paper.title: Shared Selective Persistent Memory for Agentic LLM Systems
paper.abstract: Agentic LLM systems that generate code through multi-turn tool use face a fundamental context problem: each session starts from zero, discarding the domain constraints, data schemas, tool configurations, and output preferences that made previous sessions productive. We introduce shared selective persistent memory, an architecture that retains four categories of reusable context — task specifications, data schemas, tool configurations, and output constraints — while discarding session-specific reasoning traces, and that packages them into workspaces transferable across users under role-based access control.The resulting cost curve is non-monotonic. In a controlled replication on four public datasets, where a formatting specification is established once and then withheld, no memory completes 0/12 trials at 3.8K input tokens, selective memory completes 12/12 at 3.9K, and full conversation history completes 8/12 at 7.7K. What is kept matters more than how much is kept: the winning configuration costs essentially what the failing one does, and twice as much context does not improve on it. Both differences from no memory survive Bonferroni-corrected exact McNemar tests (p = 0.0005, p = 0.008); selective memory and full history are indistinguishable on completion (p = 0.125) and separate on price. Every no-memory failure is a specification failure and nothing else — the artifacts are structurally sound but do not reproduce a constraint they were never given.We implement this in a deployed platform where agents produce git-versioned artifacts from CSV, SQL, REST, and MCP sources. A complementary zero-token data refresh contract decouples generated programs from runtime data, firing on 12/12 trials at a median 0.08s with no model call, while summary-driven data representation costs 97–431x fewer tokens than raw injection. Across 24 recurring enterprise tasks selective memory completes 23/24 against 19/24 and 17/24, though at that sample no pairwise difference reaches significance; there, where users re-specify rather than rely on memory, full history returns no improvement at all despite 9x the input.

paper.title: Hydra: Adaptive Adversarial Attacks for Dynamic Multi-Stage Edge Intelligence Services

author.affiliation: national university of singaore, National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Modern edge AI systems rely on dynamic, multi-stage pipelines vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing attacks primarily target static tasks and lack adaptability to these complex environments. We propose Hydra, an adversarial attack framework for AI-driven video streaming and edge security services. Hydra integrates three innovations: Multi-Stage Service Disruption (MSSD) that coherently misleads successive pipeline components, Resource-Aware Transferability Enhancement (RATE) for effective attacks under edge constraints, and Meta-Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Perturbation (MetaRAP) that dynamically tunes attack parameters based on real-time system states. Evaluations on a multimodal medical RAG system demonstrate Hydra’s superior efficacy, achieving up to 75% ASR against specialized retrievers at \epsilon=8/255, a 12% absolute improvement over baselines. Hydra also exhibits strong transferability, defense robustness, and a favorable efficiency trade-off, requiring only 2.1 seconds per adversarial example. This work highlights a potent threat to edge intelligence services, urging development of robust multi-stage defenses.

paper.title: Silent Locale Corruption: Diagnosing and Mitigating Chinese-Locale Semantic Failures in LLM Tool Calling
paper.abstract: When a language-model agent fills tool-call arguments, the argument value is the action: 转一万二 ("transfer twelve thousand") must become transfer(12000), and 两斤苹果 ("two jin of apples") must become order(weight_kg=1.0). We show that today’s LLMs silently corrupt such values when Chinese locale semantics must be converted into canonical arguments — producing schema-valid, confidently wrong actions that no validator catches. We introduce ZhToolLocale, a diagnostic benchmark with machine-computed gold values (lunar-calendar libraries, deterministic numeral and unit parsers), paraphrase triplets, and a pre-registered audit protocol; we report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and significance tests for every headline claim. Across six models from five families — including two Chinese-trained — we find: (1) lunar-calendar conversion degrades significantly in every model (all p ≤ .031) and catastrophically in five of six (0–28%, vs. ~100% on fixed-date controls); a pre-registered matched-pair control refuted our initial memorization hypothesis — explicit lunar dates are, if anything, easier than festival names — indicating genuine conversion difficulty rather than recall; (2) Chinese-centric training confers a sizable advantage at the large tier (deepseek-chat: 93.3% overall, 81% lunar — the strongest model tested) but does not rescue the 7B tier (qwen2.5: lunar 3%); (3) paraphrase disagreement detects scattered errors (precision up to 0.92) but is structurally blind to consistent mis-conversion, which we quantify; (4) a deterministic converter restores 94.8–100% accuracy with significant gains for three models (all p ≤ .0012), but routing is tier-governed: frontier models route voluntarily (93–99%), a mid-tier model improves only under an explicit mandate, and two 7–8B models cannot be made to route at all (gains non-significant) — implying that deployable-tier safety must be architectural rather than prompted. We release the benchmark as a generator whose golds are computed on demand, with a per-category deployment card.

paper.title: Self-Correcting Large Language Models: Generation vs. Multiple Choice
paper.abstract: Large language models have recently demonstrated remarkable abilities to self-correct their responses through iterative refinement, often referred to as self-consistency or self-reflection. However, the dynamics of this self-correction mechanism may differ substantially depending on whether the model is tasked with open-ended text generation or with selecting the most appropriate response from multiple predefined options. In this paper, we conduct a systematic investigation of these two paradigms by comparing performance trends and error-correction behaviors across question answering tasks, covering language models of different scales and families. Our experimental results reveal distinct patterns of improvement and failure modes:While open-ended generation often benefits from the flexibility of re-interpretation and compositional refinement, multiple-choice selection can leverage clearer solution boundaries but may be limited by the provided options. This contrast also reflects the dual demands faced by emerging agentic LLM applications: effective agents must not only generate and refine open-ended plans or explanations, but also make reliable discrete choices when operating within constrained action spaces. Our findings, therefore, highlight that the design of self-correction mechanisms should take into account the interaction between task structure and output space, with implications for both knowledge-intensive reasoning and decision-oriented applications of LLMs.

paper.title: Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories
paper.abstract: Persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. We present a controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories, and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to \leq10–15pp via equivalence testing). A failure-mode triage reveals why: agents fail on implementation skill—feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring—not missing repository knowledge that a context file could supply; a manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. We further show that borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman \rho=0.75), offering a candidate explanation for prior contradictions: single-agent studies draw tasks from different agents’ informative bands. We release all code, data, and analysis.

paper.title: Causal Decomposition of LLM Agent Failure via Oracle-State Intervention

author.affiliation: Computer Science Department, Stanford University and Algoverse Coding Academy LLC

paper.abstract: LLM agents degrade as trajectories lengthen, motivating current research on context management methods that compress, filter, or restructure history. All of these methods share the untested assumption that context degradation is the primary bottleneck of agentic systems. To test this hypothesis, we introduce an oracle-state intervention framework that decomposes agent failure modes, isolates context as a causal variable by replacing a failing agent’s accumulated history with ground-truth structured state, and measures recovery. Across 420 failed WebArena trajectories with two models (Qwen3.5-27B and GPT-5.2), we find that context management is effective but not in the way commonly assumed in recent literature. In the default WebArena Qwen and GPT configurations, replacing context after failure recovers under 10% of failed trajectories. Additionally, independent human annotators attribute only 11.7% of failures to context-caused errors. The remaining 58–74% of failures persist even after both context and environment are restored, and the convergence between intervention-based and human-attribution estimates suggests that context availability explains only a minority of failures. Yet continuous oracle state throughout the trajectory improves success by 19-38%, and the gap between oracle-maintained and self-generated state widens from 7% to 18% as trajectories lengthen. This causal intervention framework reveals that post hoc context repair rarely rescues failed agents, while continuously maintained privileged state improves long horizon execution. Moreover, our findings suggest that progress on agentic systems will require improving planning and execution capabilities alongside context engineering, rather than treating context quality as the dominant bottleneck.

paper.title: Measuring the Serving Stack Instead of the Model: Hidden Confounds in Local Tool-Use Evaluation
paper.abstract: A coding agent must emit a valid tool call—a parseable invocation of a tool in the provided schema—before the harness can execute its chosen action. We study how local serving stacks affect this protocol step and show that measured outcomes can depend on the serving layer rather than model behavior alone. In Ollama, the default tools= request is gated per model by a static template flag: some models are accepted and return calls as text, some return native tool_calls, while Phi-3 and Gemma-3 are rejected before inference. In our harness, rejection and retry exhaustion are not preserved as structured failure metadata, so downstream analysis can misclassify them as model non-calls and naively report 0% fidelity. Adding a text tool list while retaining the native channel recovers much of the measured fidelity for accepted models, whereas a uniform text protocol reduces fidelity for Llama-3.2, which has native tool-call support. Cross-stack probes on Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang show different handling of the same request. Constrained decoding removes parse failures but can induce non-termination, and turn-pooled versus per-instance estimates differ by up to about 55 points. We conclude with a checklist for treating serving behavior as part of the evaluation protocol.

paper.title: Authentic but Not Neutral: Selective Evidence in LLM-Agent Leaderboards
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used as agents that interact with tools and environments to carry out complex tasks. This development has prompted a growing range of benchmarks and leaderboards for comparing agent performance. Yet the evidence behind these comparisons is not always fully disclosed. Even when every disclosed record is authentic and correctly scored, a reporter with access to the complete ledger can choose a favorable subset. We study whether rank claims remain informative under such adaptive release. An authenticated disclosure frame fixes systems, denominators, bundle bounds, and the canonical claim universe before selection. Worst-case completion keeps every reported edge sound, but a budgeted reporter can still choose which comparisons become certifiable. This separates the soundness of reported comparisons from neutrality in what gets reported. Across four public agent-evaluation ledgers, target-directed release produces positive attention gaps for most eligible targets at intermediate budgets; the effect depends on budget and bundle layout and disappears under an equal-per-system quota in one ledger. We derive an exact polynomial algorithm for the unit-cost target problem and prove weak NP-completeness under heterogeneous costs. These experiments are structural stress tests, not evidence that benchmark maintainers select evidence strategically. They show that certificate soundness does not imply disclosure neutrality.

paper.title: GRASP: Generating, Revising, and Assessing for Strategic Planning with Agentic AI
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) typically exhibit a performance profile where reliability degrades as task complexity increases. We address the challenge of generating high-quality natural language executable plans for complex tasks by introducing GRASP, a strategy-aware, multi-stage planning framework. GRASP decouples the planning pipeline across specialized, context-isolated modules: it pre-compiles global macro-guidelines (GenPlan), explores alternative localized strategies within isolated context windows (RevPlan), and independently evaluates trajectories using a multi-criteria discriminator (VerPlan). Empirical evaluations show that GRASP consistently establishes a new state-of-the-art frontier across diverse datasets, yielding substantial accuracy gains over direct LLM planners on Natural Plan Calendar Scheduling (\sim12.4%\uparrow), ZebraLogic (\sim30.8%\uparrow), and SciBench Math. Crucially, under multi-task scaling—where standard planners suffer immediate performance collapse—GRASP completely flattens the multi-task degradation penalty. In interleaved dual-task environments, GRASP achieves an absolute accuracy gain of up to 16.7% over direct LLM planners. Furthermore, by isolating context and enforcing strict macro-regularization, GRASP outperforms frontier reasoning models (such as GPT-5-mini) by a margin of 14.5%.

paper.title: Answer or Compute? Direct Inference vs. Code Generation for LLM Game-State Understanding in RTS Games
paper.abstract: A large language model (LLM) can understand a game state in two ways: answer questions about it directly, or write a program that computes the answer. We compare these modalities on three real-time-strategy tasks—factual extraction, strategic assessment, and win prediction—holding states, questions, and models fixed. On mechanical questions, code wins decisively: hit-point (HP) aggregation rises from 30% to 100%, and the direct-mode failures are mostly a refusal to declare ties, not bad arithmetic. On judgment tasks, code seemed to win as well, until a trivial baseline exposed why: on snapshots from bot games the material leader always wins, so sign(ΣHP) alone scores 100%. On contested states built to remove this artifact, no arm—direct, chain-of-thought, or code-based—reliably beats chance (40 tests, Holm-corrected), while a simple unit-count cue reaches 72%. Code makes LLMs reliable aggregators; it does not make them judges. We contribute the shortcut audit and hard-set construction that judgment benchmarks built on game traces should adopt.

paper.title: Foundation First: Stabilizing SLM Agents via Pre-execution Logical Scaffolding
paper.abstract: In on-device agentic systems, Small Language Models (SLMs) are essential for ensuring privacy-preserving personalization and low-latency execution. However, despite their capacity to handle isolated atomic tasks, during complex multi-step orchestration SLMs frequently suffer from stochastic drift—a phenomenon where minor logical deviations cascade into irrecoverable trajectory failures. In this work, we demonstrate the primacy of pre-execution planning, revealing that mitigating initial logical drift is vastly more effective than mid-trajectory interventions. Building on this insight, we propose FORST(FOundation fiRST) framework that implements sequential logical scaffolding in pre-execution planning, where predefined expert anchors are injected as fixed pre-computed KV-cache states. While the scaffolding ensures logical stability, KV-cache reuse efficiently realizes the structured anchor prefix without repeatedly prefilling static anchors. Then, we can maintain a monolithic reasoning chain within predefined logical planning boundaries and effectively eliminate the redundant computational overhead of structured anchors. Extensive evaluations on the MCPEval benchmark demonstrate that establishing this rigid logical foundation via achieves competitive or numerically higher performance than frontier models, while achieving an latency reduction on edge-device platforms.

paper.title: Agent Step Value: Auditing Evaluation-Channel Sensitivity in Black-Box Agent Traces

author.affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Reusing evaluator-derived step rewards across evaluation channels raises a measurement question: does the assigned direction remain stable? We define Agent Step Value (ASV) as a channel-indexed before/after target-margin gain and identify the state-by-channel interaction from a matched 2 × 2 design. Across frozen PubMed question-answering transitions, cross-channel gain signs disagree on 48.3% of comparisons, compared with 0.3% for same-channel retries. Transition interactions are nearly balanced in sign (median +0.014; 10% trimmed mean -0.033), but asymmetric negative magnitudes produce a positive direct mean and a negative generated-view mean under the empirical target mixture. Equal-target weighting preserves a negative mean interaction but not this strict mean reversal. Matched retrieval designs localize the negative component to the generated-view coordinate and retain its direction across three sign checks that vary readout and evaluator stack. In a matched 512-token source-contract follow-up, source-only generation restores the positive mean direction on artifact-bearing retrievals and removes parser-detected support claims from artifact-free before-state views. These results support an explanation in which generated support inflates the pre-retrieval baseline. The resulting audit can localize channel sensitivity and test an intervention before step rewards are reused.

paper.title: FUSE: Failure-Guided Scenario Synthesis and Weighted Refinement for LLM Function Calling
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on function calling to act across multi-turn interactions, but compact models remain brittle when tool availability, required parameters, and dialogue constraints change over time. Existing synthetic tool-use data often broadens coverage without targeting the recurring failures of a specific model. We present FUSE, a failure-guided refinement approach that uses the model’s own function-calling errors to synthesize harder training scenarios and then emphasizes difficult examples during supervised fine-tuning. This data-centric design turns diagnostic failures into targeted training signal while remaining simple to apply with standard offline fine-tuning. Experiments on BFCLv3 show that FUSE substantially improves a compact Qwen3-based model across standard and stress categories, including missing functions, missing parameters, and long-context interactions. Evaluation on BFCLv4 provides initial evidence that the same refinement strategy can transfer to selected agentic function-calling tasks.

paper.title: Is Progressive Disclosure All You Need for Long-Context Agents?

author.affiliation: University of Hong Kong and University of California, Davis

paper.abstract: Long-document question answering usually forces a choice between loading the whole document into the context window and bolting on a separate retriever. Agentic AI suggests a broader option, giving the agent the document path and letting it decide how and what to read. Agent Skills, a standard for packaging expertise into folders an agent loads on demand, supply a ready mechanism: progressive disclosure, which exposes only what a query needs, from a short description down to the specific passages. Practitioners rapidly adopted this pattern for book-length understanding tasks, but the evidence to support such choices has been anecdotal. We run the first controlled study of the pattern, comparing raw-document navigation and several designs of Agent Skills packs against a classical hybrid retriever across three agent harnesses and three model families on \inftyBench. On a single book, the gain depends on the harness, running large when the agent navigates the raw document poorly but near zero when a strong agent harness already divides and retrieves on its own. When scaling up to tasks that span many books, raw-document navigation collapses while one-level progressive disclosure degrades more slowly and pulls ahead. A second, deeper routing level never helps and sometimes breaks accuracy outright, so one level is enough. Progressive disclosure buys context, not intelligence: it is redundant while a strong agent can locate the right passages itself, and decisive once the corpus grows too large to navigate by reading.

paper.title: From Credit Assignment to Repair: A Leakage-Controlled Diagnostic Study of Tool-Using Agents
paper.abstract: End-of-trajectory rewards do not identify the decision associated with a tool-agent failure. We treat step-level credit assignment as failure localization and test whether it supports selective repair. Silver labels come only from completed training trajectories. Prefix-only classifiers use task-grouped model selection and remain frozen during evaluation. On the retail domain of \tau^2-bench, the selected classifier reaches 46.4% out-of-fold F1 and 61.1% F1 on 60 held-out trajectories comprising 333 scored decisions. The frozen gate selects 101 decisions, but the verifier changes actions in only seven trajectories. None changes binary reward relative to its task-matched baseline. Airline and telecom produce no changed trajectory. Mean reward differences are small, and every task-clustered confidence interval includes zero across the three domains. An exact replay audit reproduces 60 telecom baseline trajectories but triggers no intervention. The evidence identifies a localization–repair gap: detecting suspicious decisions does not yield repair without calibrated treatment coverage, grounded alternatives, and controlled attribution.

paper.title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
paper.abstract: LLM memory systems often filter facts classified as stale from the current prompt. We study this query-time context filtering, without deleting stored memories, in memory-conditioned question answering. Across three models on a synthetic benchmark, controlled label corruption moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of −0.176 to −0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show greater degradation from false-drop than false-keep; retaining evidence can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On one frozen 102/102 calibration/test query split, empirical policy selection using labeled calibration outcomes reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. A question-disjoint MemoryAgentBench replication is inconclusive: gain +0.03, 95% CI [−0.01, +0.08]. These results establish a controlled sensitivity mechanism, not generalization to long-horizon agents. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics. Context filtering should be cost-sensitive and validated on matched labeled data; label-free retention is an accuracy fallback under the tested errors, subject to separate privacy and retention requirements.

paper.title: STAC: When Innocent Tools Form Dangerous Chains for LLM Agents
paper.abstract: As LLMs advance into autonomous agents with tool-use capabilities, they introduce security challenges that extend beyond traditional content-based LLM safety concerns. This paper introduces Sequential Tool Attack Chaining (STAC), a novel multi-turn attack framework that exploits agent tool use. STAC chains together tool calls that each appears harmless in isolation but, when combined, collectively enable harmful operations that only become apparent at the final execution step. We apply our framework to automatically generate and systematically evaluate 483 STAC cases, featuring 1,352 sets of user-agent-environment interactions and spanning diverse domains, tasks, agent types, and 10 failure modes. Our evaluations show that state-of-the-art LLM agents are highly vulnerable to STAC, with attack success rates (ASR) exceeding 90% in most cases. The core design of STAC’s automated framework is a closed-loop pipeline that synthesizes executable multi-step tool chains, validates them through in-environment execution, and reverse-engineers stealthy multi-turn prompts that reliably induce agents to execute the verified malicious sequence. We further perform defense analysis and find that existing prompt-based defenses provide limited protection. To address this gap, we propose a new reasoning-driven defense prompt that achieves the strongest initial-turn protection, cutting ASR by up to 28.8%; however, this advantage erodes sharply under adaptive attacks, and an experience-based defense (ToolShield) proves more durable over sustained multi-turn interactions. These results highlight a crucial gap: defending tool-enabled agents requires reasoning over entire action sequences and their cumulative effects, rather than evaluating isolated prompts or responses. Data and code: https://github.com/amazon-science/MultiTurnAgentAttack.

paper.title: Do Query-Agnostic Memory Structures Earn Their Budget? A 10M-Token Audit with Exact Read Limits
paper.abstract: Long-term memory systems often organize experience before future queries are known, but whether this improves evidence access under a fixed read budget remains unclear. We evaluate inexpensive query-agnostic segmentation and hierarchical retrieval on AMA-Bench agent trajectories and BEAM conversations spanning 128K to 10M tokens. Experiments use exact serialized-context budgets, development-only tuning, two sentence encoders, and uncertainty estimates clustered by trajectory or conversation. In an exploratory post-plan analysis of 1,117 step-anchored trajectory questions, fixed three-turn windows outperform all tested alternative boundary methods. On BEAM, primary-encoder flat retrieval recall falls from 0.564 at 128K to 0.331 at 10M. Single-vector hierarchical routing further reduces recall; multiple local vectors recover part of this loss but do not surpass flat retrieval. Doubling the read budget from 8,000 to 16,000 characters improves evidence recall at every scale with both encoders. However, the 10M evaluation, comprising 130 questions from eight conversations, detects no corresponding QA improvement. Single-vector routing reduces QA accuracy, while multi-vector routing is not distinguishable from flat retrieval. These findings identify coarse representation quality as a bottleneck in the tested hierarchies and show that improved evidence access need not yield better answers.

paper.title: Explicit State Elicitation Is Not Enough: A Controlled Audit of Memory-Policy Classification
paper.abstract: Personalized agents must decide whether retrieved user memory should be used, ignored, updated, or queried before it affects a task. We develop an empirical audit protocol for structured intermediate outputs: auditing dataset shortcuts, isolating bundled prompt changes, testing answer-associated labels and decomposed evidence, and retaining provider-level execution failures. A 480-example synthetic development set initially suggested large gains from a state-structured prompt bundle, but TF-IDF diagnostics showed lexical separability and no positive standalone Ignore cases. We therefore build a frozen 160-example controlled counterfactual set with 40 matched four-way families and rule-derived reference policies. There, exposing four state definitions improves accuracy, but adding an isolated explicit state-output field does not significantly improve policy accuracy for Llama-3.3-70B and gives only a marginal, non-significant gain for GPT-OSS-120B. Supplying benchmark-associated state labels shifts policy predictions; because those labels deterministically map to policies, this is label-conditioning, not evidence of a faithful mechanism. Family-level and seed-stability analyses show that example accuracy overstates counterfactual consistency. A decomposed semantic-evidence follow-up does not improve routing for the cleanly evaluated endpoint, while the GPT-OSS condition fails provider-side request validation. We evaluate policy classification only.

paper.title: Retrieval is Enough: A Memory-Augmented Agent for Algorithm Selection

author.affiliation: national university of singaore, National University of Singapore
national university of singaore, National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Selecting the best algorithm for each optimization instance is difficult because algorithm performance can vary substantially across instance structures and parameter settings. Existing learned selectors often encode historical experience in fixed model parameters, making new performance records costly to incorporate. We introduce a memory augmented agent for instance wise algorithm selection based on retrieval augmented generation. Given a new instance, the agent retrieves structurally similar historical cases, each containing the complete performance profile of all candidate options rather than only the winning label. It then reasons over the retrieved objective gaps and rankings before invoking an algorithm and configuration. New verified records can be added directly to the external memory without retraining the selector. We evaluate the proposed approach on 10{,}898 geographically grounded hub location instances, using 8{,}718 instances for retrieval and 2{,}180 for testing across five algorithm and configuration options. The proposed method achieves 68.35% selection accuracy and a 0.549% objective gap relative to the virtual best solver, outperforming the single best solver and retrieval only label voting baselines. These results demonstrate the value of combining retrieval with reasoning over complete solver performance records.

paper.title: Decomposing Self-Reflection in LLM Agents: Diagnostic Scaffolds, Uncertainty Labels, and Action Diversity
paper.abstract: Self-reflective agents typically bundle monitoring language with a downstream control policy, making it difficult to identify why reflection changes behavior. We present a six-condition ablation that separates evidence re-exposure, diagnostic questions, uncertainty labels, differentiated follow-up actions, and diagnosis–action alignment. Our testbed is an LLM forecasting agent evaluated with Llama-3.3-70B on 310 armed-conflict escalation cases, plus supplementary GPT-4o and 12-country transfer probes. Diagnostic questions produce comparable F1 to free reflection (0.296 vs. 0.297), and adding a seven-label taxonomy while holding the action fixed changes F1 by only +0.008. The closest matched comparison for action differentiation is taxonomy-only versus random action assignment (F vs. D), which holds the typed monitor and taxonomy fixed while replacing the shared-action policy with randomly varying substantive actions: F1 rises from 0.304 to 0.338. Type-matched routing reaches 0.379, but we detect no significant advantage over random assignment (C vs. D, p=0.714). This underpowered contrast does not establish equivalence; it prevents assigning the gain specifically to matching. Brier scores remain flat and transfer is unreliable. Thus, richer reflective traces do not establish better agent control. Our results motivate controls matched for information, vocabulary, and actions when attributing gains in reflection pipelines and identify simple action perturbations as a necessary baseline for type-specific policies.

paper.title: Agent-Readiness of Synthesized API Tools: Parametric Gravity and the Limits of Documentation Grounding

author.affiliation: Rheinisch Westfälische Technische Hochschule Aachen and Shanghai Jiaotong University
University of Amsterdam, University of Amsterdam

paper.abstract: We study whether LLM agents can autonomously synthesize deployment-ready MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers from raw REST API documentation, and whether the resulting servers are reliable enough for downstream agentic task completion. Evaluating 8 synthesis models across 14 APIs under three documentation conditions — full docs, no docs, and counterfactually mutated docs — we find that synthesis is broadly feasible: 11 of 14 APIs achieve sufficient tool coverage, and synthesized servers match or exceed human-authored references. The dominant mediating factor is not model capability but parametric gravity: for well-known APIs (GitHub, Stripe, Shopify), training-time knowledge overrides in-context documentation, rendering documentation provision neutral or harmful. A counterfactual mutation study confirms this: high-familiarity APIs show near-zero adherence to renamed parameters, while low-familiarity APIs show near-complete adherence. Logit-lens probing shows the representations of memory and context become increasingly separable in the final transformer layers, consistent with deep feed-forward MLP modules as the site of parametric association storage. Synthesis coverage (SYNTH) correlates strongly with agent task completion (r = 0.937), providing a reliable pre-flight quality signal without requiring agent evaluation.

paper.title: CAPSafe: A Benchmark for Contextual Action and Plan Safety Reasoning in Embodied Agents

author.affiliation: University of Cambridge and University of Cambridge

paper.abstract: Reasoning about safety is essential for embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety benchmark (CAPSafe), designed to evaluate safety reasoning at two levels: (1) an action-level dataset that tests whether a single action is safe given its environmental context, and (2) a plan-level dataset that evaluates whether agents can generate safe long-horizon plans for complex hazardous household tasks. CAPSafe models safety conditions where hazards are situational (inferred from object properties), multiple hazards can co-occur within the same environment, and each is annotated with a relative severity level for fine-grained analysis. Evaluating nine closed and open-source LLMs reveals a substantial gap between hazard recognition and safe long-horizon planning. Several models achieve high accuracy in recognizing unsafe actions (exceeding 90% in the best cases), yet safe long-horizon planning remains substantially harder. Gemini-3-pro achieves the highest safe success rate (78.19%), while other models remain below 65%. These results highlight that robust safety reasoning over long action sequences remains an open challenge.

paper.title: Where the Tokens Go: A Measured Anatomy of LLM Agent Trajectory Costs
paper.abstract: Tool-using agents repeatedly transmit prompts and conversation history, but aggregate token counts obscure which components drive cost. We introduce a five-component accounting convention for append-only agent loops, using provider usage records and fixed-prefix token-count probes without a local tokenizer. With prompt caching disabled, in 954 episodes (4891 requests) from one claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 model across three synthetic task families, the recurring fixed prefix accounts for 76.6% of baseline input tokens. Tool schemas contribute 69.1%, echoed assistant output 6.5%, and the tool-result residual, including framing, 16.9%. A descriptive fit to continuing episodes gives per-step input growth of about 363 tokens; longer-horizon cost ratios are extrapolations. Across the same 144 tasks, family-informed tool pruning reduces mean cost by 24.1% with a success difference of -1.4 percentage points (paired 95% CI [-3.5, 0.0]). A rolling history window saves 2.0% with identical observed outcomes. Truncating results at 600 characters reduces success from 98.6% to 47.2% while more than doubling mean cost alongside longer unsuccessful episodes. These findings apply to the tested model, mock tools, and short horizons. The accompanying package reproduces the analysis from frozen usage logs and prefix counts.

paper.title: Feedback Blindness: Diagnosing Silent Failures in Closed-Loop Agentic Data-Generation Pipelines

author.affiliation: Hanoi University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Closed-loop synthetic-data pipelines combine planning, LLM generation, verification, and deduplication; accepted outputs steer later generation. We study a production pipeline for Vietnamese contact-center compliance data and identify feedback blindness: an internal feedback mechanism stops serving its intended function while every stage completes normally, leaving only downstream metric degradation as evidence. We diagnose four instances: cumulative-count eviction empties a recency window; batch-level deduplication misses candidates scored before any batch member is committed; static boundary exemplars repeatedly anchor generation; and a fixed-size anti-repeat reference set loses informativeness as the dataset grows. We describe architecture-level fixes, mechanism-specific health signals, and a controlled ablation and scaling evaluation. The central lesson is that aggregate duplicate and acceptance rates are insufficient for diagnosis; pipelines should also monitor the feedback mechanisms that produce those outcomes.

paper.title: Tool Quality, Not Framework Complexity: Evaluating RLM Vision, Code, and Memory Pipelines for Radiology Applications

author.affiliation: Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg and Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg

paper.abstract: It remains unclear whether agentic augmentation (iterative tool use, code execution, or retrieved memory) improves over single-pass VLM inference for medical image interpretation. We present a systematic quantitative evaluation of the Recursive Language Model (RLM) framework on a multimodal medical task, comparing three pipeline architectures (P1 direct vision, P2 iterative RLM tool use, P3 model-written code agent) across four retrieval-augmented memory conditions on 100 CheXpert Plus chest X-rays, scoring with CheXbert (14-label classification) and GREEN (radiology-specific LLM judge). Three findings emerge: (1) direct vision outperforms both agentic variants; the RLM loop consumes 7-9× more tokens without adding task-relevant information when its only tool calls the same VLM; (2) retrieval consistently helps, but the optimal pool size depends on metric and pipeline: top-5 is the sweet spot for direct-vision report quality (GREEN +37%), while 24 retrieved cases further benefit pathology classification (CheXbert +50%) and can improve GREEN for agentic pipelines; and (3) qualitative analysis shows code agents with a pretrained classifier succeed when it returns confident pathology scores but fail on normal cases where it returns noise-floor outputs, illustrating that tool quality, not framework complexity, determines outcome.

paper.title: Autonomous Event Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale

author.affiliation: national university of singaore, National University of Singapore and SAP SE

paper.abstract: Enterprise agent language models must coordinate specialist agents over continuous business-event streams, yet most multi-agent evaluations assume discrete request-response workflows. We present a controlled simulation based on a sanitized enterprise research snapshot: 208 scenarios, 393 events, and 1,051 expected agent calls across Persona (<10 agents), Department (20–80), and Enterprise (200) registries. We compare DAG Plan Execute with ReAct and evaluate a minimal Task Manager for priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Both systems perform well on the Persona cohort but score lower on the Enterprise cohort, especially for Simple scenarios; a larger, more confusable discovery space may contribute. The tested DAG Plan Execute implementation generally maintains higher agent-call precision, whereas ReAct shows stronger recall and Expected Answer Completeness in several Enterprise conditions. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14–75% and improves related-event Expected Answer Completeness by over 20 percentage points at Enterprise scale. These controlled simulation results characterize the tested systems but do not establish production readiness.

paper.title: ToolMisuseBench: An Offline Deterministic Benchmark for Tool Misuse and Recovery in Agentic Systems
paper.abstract: Reliable tool use is a fundamental capability for agentic systems, yet existing evaluations primarily focus on successful tool execution and provide limited insight into how agents recover from tool failures. To address this gap, we introduce ToolMisuseBench, an offline deterministic benchmark for evaluating tool misuse and fault-conditioned recovery. ToolMisuseBench evaluates recovery behavior across domains, fault types, and difficulty levels, using output-grounded success criteria and typed recoverability metadata. The seed-42 release includes 6,000 training, 900 development, and 1,200 public-test tasks covering CRUD, retrieval, file operations, and scheduling, including failures such as timeouts, rate limits, hidden first-call schema perturbations, authorization errors, and adversarial responses. Using the benchmark, we evaluate deterministic reference agents together with local 3-4B tool-calling LLMs (Qwen3-4B, Ministral-3B, and Llama-3.2-3B). On the public-test split, Parser+Repair achieves 0.767 task success and 0.736 conditional recovery success, compared with 0.158 task success when recovery is disabled. On a shared stratified 216-task diagnostic panel, Qwen3-4B, Ministral-3B, and Llama-3.2-3B achieve task success rates of 0.796, 0.903, and 0.773, respectively. Fault-level analysis reveals distinct recovery weaknesses that overall task success alone fails to capture. ToolMisuseBench provides a controlled and reproducible framework for diagnosing tool-use recovery under frozen fault plans, enabling more rigorous evaluation of robust tool-using agents beyond execution accuracy.

paper.title: Same Answers, Different Active-Store States: An Identification Audit of FactConsolidation Single-Hop
paper.abstract: After a factual conflict, the same credited answer can arise from different record-choice rules and different active-store states. We audit this ambiguity in MemoryAgentBench’s 400-question FactConsolidation Single-Hop (FC-SH) task. A fixed exact-template parser identifies 282 questions with two target arrivals and distinct values, plus 118 singletons. In every two-arrival case, the larger serial also arrives last, so last-arrival and maximum-serial selection coincide. We cross these selectors with stores that expose either one active record or all versions. Given this alignment and the policy contracts, all four policies produce the same 400 prediction strings and receive 393/400, although the exact earlier fact ID is visible on 0/282 targets under one-record stores and 282/282 under all-version stores. Swapping the two arrivals while preserving their serials separates the selectors on all 282 targets. Under this primary parser, seven gold items are credited only to the earlier value; joining both candidates yields 400/400 under substring exact match. Thus, within this controlled grid, released FC-SH answers identify neither record choice nor active-store visibility. This release-level measurement audit pairs an order contrast for choice with direct store observation for visibility.

paper.title: Externalizing Requirement-to-Repair Artifacts as Observable Traces for LLM-Based Program Repair
paper.abstract: Repository-level repair requires not only correct patches but also inspectable records that explain how issue requirements are translated into code changes and post-edit evidence. We contribute THEMIS, a stage-aware repair workflow that externalizes this requirement-to-repair process through semantic interpretation, a runtime requirement–code graph, graph-derived Developer guidance, retained repair rationale and patches, and post-edit audit records. A retrospective audit of 300 SWE-bench Lite cases demonstrates that these artifacts provide broad support for cross-stage inspection: a complete Developer rationale is available for 288 cases, and 214 cases (71.3%) retain a complete audited field set connecting the selected stages. The retained records further enable systematic measurement of cross-stage correspondence: target symbols recur in 62.6% of Developer rationales and in 62.8% of patches, rising to 75.8% when related symbols are included. In a paired 100-case comparison, the relational workflow resolves 19 cases versus 9 for the direct same-input condition, corresponding to a 10-percentage-point improvement. Together, these results show that THEMIS turns otherwise implicit requirement-to-repair transitions into observable traces, enabling systematic inspection of how repair decisions persist, align, and evolve across stages.

paper.title: Flight to Mediocrity: Why LLM Agent Selectors Under-Hire Experts When Quality Claims Are Unverified
paper.abstract: AI systems increasingly let one model choose another: an orchestrator routing a task to a sub-agent, or an agent picking a tool from a registry, by self-described ability. What happens when that self-report cannot be checked? In MATCHMARKET, a client hires one of three candidates whose true competence is hidden (2, 5, or 8 of 10), earning the competence of its hire. Candidates are themselves language models, inflating claims under an audit-and-fine incentive. Selectors rarely fall for the loudest liar, picking the inflator only 8–15% of the time. They fail by fleeing to mediocrity: 75–89% of their mistaken hires land on a safe, moderate candidate, not on the liar. A trivial yardstick makes the cost concrete: believing the highest claim earns 6.72 of a possible 8.0, and no selector we test significantly beats it. The best merely matches it, while the weakest fall significantly below (pooled 5.99, paired p = .002; random scores 5.0). A verified record recovers much of the loss, but only for selectors near chance without it, widening rather than closing cross-model gaps. Every outcome is scored arithmetically, no LLM judge. Unverified capability advertisement behaves like a market for lemons whose cost falls on the honest, capable provider.

paper.title: Translating the Translator: Decomposing the Cost of English-Forced Inter-Agent Communication
paper.abstract: Multi-agent LLM architectures, such as LangChain and AutoGen, largely assume English as the lingua franca for internal inter-agent communication, even when the end-user task is non-English. We fill this gap by evaluating a two-agent extraction-answer core, with an additional back-translation agent in the English-forced condition, across four typologically diverse languages (Hindi, Chinese, Spanish, Arabic; n=300 per language) using the Aya-23-8B model. We compare a native-language pipeline to an English-forced one (which incorporates a final back-translation step from English to the user’s language). We discover a statistically significant English-Forcing Tax (surviving a strict Bonferroni correction) that isolates the cost of English routing from general multi-agent orchestration overhead. Forcing inter-agent communication through English reduces Exact Match accuracy by 13.0 percentage points (Spanish) up to 30.6 percentage points (Hindi) compared to native-language multi-agent execution. Using chrF scores as a diagnostic measure of English-reference lexical overlap, we find that lower overlap is strongly associated with pipeline failure, consistent with translation loss being an important contributor to the observed performance drop. These findings suggest a compelling case for native-language routing in agent frameworks when the source and target languages are typologically distant, reducing a compounding translation tax.

paper.title: Mo’ Models, Mo’ Problems: How to best select model pools when designing Multi-Agent Systems
paper.abstract: Multi-agent Systems (MAS) combine multiple model outputs to solve complex reasoning tasks. However, despite rapid growth of available open-source models, there is limited research on how to select optimal model candidates out of this massive pool. We systematically evaluate 8 model selection strategies (including model size, accuracy and answer diversity) across before-generation (routing) and after-generation (majority-voting, LLM-as-a-judge) MAS architectures on challenging scientific benchmarks. Our findings show a significant gap between theoretical oracle potential and actual performance: Expanding candidate pool sizes often degrades performance below that of the top performing base-model. We find that candidate selection within a single model family is the strategy that yields the best relative performance over a standalone model. These results demonstrate that adding arbitrary models to a heterogeneous MAS may introduce system instability, highlighting model selection as a critical design choice for multi-agent systems.

paper.title: Be Careful Who You Trust: Coordination Dynamics under Corrupted Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Games

author.affiliation: University College London, University of London
University College London, University of London

paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as interacting agents, but it remains unclear how robust their coordination is when public communication is unreliable. We study this question in iterated N-player Stag Hunt games played by homogeneous LLM groups under controlled programmatic action inversion, which changes both the public transcript and the actions used for execution. Across an experimental grid spanning group sizes, coordination thresholds, corruption levels, and seven LLMs, we observe three main patterns. First, honest agents’ pre-flip Stag choices decline as corruption increases, but the sharp fall in public success is primarily mechanical. In the focal N=5,M=3 setting, pre-flip success remains 78% at 80% corruption, while public success falls to 12%. Second, honest choices are associated with the public history available at decision time, particularly under high corruption. Third, three threshold-style public-report benchmarks yield similar action-match rates to the LLM agents, showing substantial descriptive agreement between LLM decisions and these benchmarks. Overall, our results show that original choices, public actions, and executed outcomes must be separated when evaluating multi-agent robustness, as corrupted communication can severely and predictably degrade mutually beneficial cooperation.

paper.title: Weighted Memory Tree: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated the ability to solve multi-step tasks requiring planning, tool use, and external information access, yet growing execution histories increase inference cost and expose reasoning to outdated, irrelevant, or misleading information, potentially degrading reasoning quality. Existing memory approaches organize or compress execution histories but provide limited mechanisms for deciding which memories remain active. We introduce the \textbf{Weighted Memory Tree} (\textbf{WMT}), a hierarchical memory system that organizes execution into tasks, subtasks, and actions while assigning each memory a dynamic retention score. Event-based updates and selection-based decay revise these scores, allowing WMT to preserve useful information, fold completed trajectories, suppress low-utility content, and retain access to folded context. We evaluate WMT on GAIA and its text-only subset, GAIA-Text, using Qwen3-8B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama-3.1-8B, with ablations and memory-poisoning experiments. Relative to linear memory, WMT improves accuracy by an average of 9.97 percentage points on GAIA-Text and 10.10 percentage points on GAIA, while reducing prompt-token usage by 32.8% and 32.2%, respectively. In our controlled memory-poisoning experiments, WMT reduces the measured persistence and propagation of intentionally injected unreliable information. Our results suggest that effective long-horizon agent memory depends less on storing more information than on deciding which information should remain active.

paper.title: ACIES: A Self-Evolving Agentic Contract-Based Framework for Cyber-Physical System Control Synthesis
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored in cyber-physical system design as a promising tool to facilitate the conversion of natural-language requirements into formal specifications, and the generation of plans and controllers that provably satisfy them. Existing LLM-based pipelines, however, mostly validate the designed controllers by simulation, and carry no mechanism for improving their outcomes from past designs. We present ACIES, a self-evolving agentic contract-based framework for cyber-physical system control synthesis. Given a set of system requirements, ACIES automatically generates a control architecture that realizes the requirements using a sequence of synthesis episodes. Within each episode, a Translator agent formalizes the system requirements into temporal logic, and a Decomposer agent structures them into a system-level contract and proposes a decomposition into component-level contracts that can be independently implemented. A formal verification step is then integrated in the decomposition loop to check whether the component-level contracts are consistent, compatible, and provide a correct refinement of the system-level contract. Each failed check, at the verification or implementation step, returns a diagnostic signal that drives automated contract repair at the system or the component level. Across episodes, a Summarizer agent distills verification outcomes into reusable lessons stored in a memory. Evaluation results on five control synthesis tasks with eight LLM backbones show that the formalized system requirements are successfully decomposed and mapped to a synthesizable control architecture that realizes them, while self-evolution reduces the Decomposer token consumption by up to 65% and the end-to-end synthesis latency by up to 62%.

paper.title: Capability Is Not Complementarity: A Routing Feasibility Study in Financial Question Answering
paper.abstract: Selective routing is useful only when an expensive branch solves cases that a cheaper branch misses. We call this prerequisite expert complementarity and ask whether a capable iterative agent actually provides it. In a prospectively frozen financial question answering study, we compare Static with bounded ReAct across multiple capability tiers. Within each tier, the arms share the model, answer contract, retrieval interface, scoring, and resource limits. A stronger model removes ReAct’s average deficit and brings it to parity with Static, showing that relative performance depends on model choice. Yet Static and ReAct still succeed on nearly the same items. Across 150 shared items per tier, ReAct adds only one or two unique exact successes; oracle quality headroom point estimates are at most 1.7 points, while ReAct takes 2.1 to 2.6 times as long. A stability check preserves this pattern. Capability and complementarity are therefore distinct: improving an expensive branch can make it competitive without making it useful for routing. Evaluation contracts should be harmonized and paired complementarity audited before training a selector. This result concerns bounded ReAct over controlled benchmark evidence, not iterative agents in general.

paper.title: Generation and Verification: Human-Agent Collaboration for Safety-Critical Automotive Software Engineering
paper.abstract: Research on coding agents mainly focuses on generation quality. Yet, safety-critical automotive software makes two additional demands. It prioritizes verification, since every change is reviewed, traced to a requirement, and checked against industry standards such as MISRA and AUTOSAR before it can be committed. It is also a narrow domain, written against layered architectures, embedded resource constraints, and organization-specific interface conventions that are scarce in the data general-purpose LLMs are trained on. We present a coding assistant for automotive C/C++ that addresses both demands. First, it exposes three tools to the user over the Model Context Protocol (generate, edit, and verify), allowing developers to run verify on any code on demand rather than relying on the agent to check its own output. Second, rather than using a general-purpose model, we customize the underlying LLM for the automotive domain through prompt engineering and fine-tuning. We construct a dataset from automotive production code of AUMOVIO, where each function is paired with the requirement texts and Unified Modeling Language (UML) behavior it must satisfy. In a two-week pilot on active production projects, developers report verify as the most-used tool and confirm using it on their own code and not only on generated output. Comparing model customization strategies, 75% prefer the faster prompt-engineered configuration. MISRA- and AUTOSAR-inspired pattern checkers indicate that prompt engineering achieves a lower number of violations on C, while fine-tuning shows better conformance with architecture patterns for C++.

paper.title: Two Thirds of the Best-of-K Oracle Band in Tool Agents Is Unreachable by Reward-Free Selection
paper.abstract: Running a tool agent n times and keeping the best run is worth 2.19–22.37 points on τ²-bench, a floor any scaffold spending n times the calls has to clear. Choosing among those runs, for no additional model calls, is worth anywhere from −23.68 to +12.28 depending on which rule does the choosing. We evaluate 9 selectors that read only the agent’s own trajectory across 28 model × domain cells and 10 403 released trials, and add an LLM judge that reads the trajectories but never a reward and never the evaluation criteria. Every arm is therefore reward-free: the nine rules are verifier-free as well, the judge is not, and neither sees a label. Against a mean best-of-K oracle band of 12.29 points, which is what a selector holding the reward would collect, the judge recovers 32.7% and the best free rule 21.0%, leaving 67.3% of that band unreachable without the label. One measurable property of the rollouts orders the task distributions, the no-mode rate, the share of tasks on which no two of the K rollouts emit the same write-action sequence, and what it predicts is when agreement is exploitable rather than when selection is possible. Where agreement-based rules are nearly inert the judge is worth +5.95 against +0.53; where the rollouts are undifferentiated it returns 1.19 against a band of 14.4 points; on a third domain it returns −0.64 and loses to a free heuristic costing one fewer call.

paper.title: AIDG: A Formal Decomposition of Information Extraction and Containment Asymmetries in Multi-Turn LLM Dialogue
paper.abstract: Multi-turn LLM evaluation is typically reported as a single win-rate scalar, conflating distinct capabilities. We introduce AIDG (Adversarial Information Deduction Game), formalizing multi-turn adversarial dialogue as a two-player partially observable stochastic game (POSG) and decomposing performance along Seeker (extraction) and Holder (containment) roles. The decomposition isolates three failure modes: cooperative-prior leakage, constraint–reasoning interference, and inefficient hypothesis-space traversal. Across 439 games over six frontier LLMs, defensive performance is tightly clustered (σ = 1.9 ELO) while offensive performance varies substantially (σ = 53.3 ELO); confirmation framing increases extraction odds 7.75× over uninformed deduction (p < 0.00001); and constraint violations account for 41.3% of deductive failures, uncorrelated with scale (ρ = 0.0). We position the containment-over-extraction gap not as a surprising finding but as a measurable consequence of locally-resolvable defensive decisions versus globally-coupled offensive planning, and use the decomposition to attribute the gap per model. All design choices, including turn-decay weighting and the Bradley–Terry rating model, are derived from explicit assumptions.

paper.title: V-RAM: A Visual Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Reasoning Framework for Medical Dialogue Diagnosis
paper.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) are increasingly explored for multimodal medical diagnosis, their ability to conduct accurate consultation remains challenging because of unstable visual reasoning and limited tracking of patient information across dialogue turns. To address this problem we present V-RAM (Visual Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent Reasoning Framework), a training-free framework for improving LVLM-based multimodal medical dialogue diagnosis. V-RAM improves medical dialogue diagnosis by adding visual retrieval, structured memory, and multi-agent reasoning around a pretrained LVLM. It retrieves similar medical images as diagnostic cues and tracks patient evidence across dialogue turns. The framework operates at inference time, it requires no supervised fine-tuning and can be used with different LVLM backbones. Experiments on benchmark show that V-RAM outperforms existing baselines and the current LVLMs by 7.3% on an average with 86% lesser number of turns that are used for medical dialogue diagnosis.

paper.title: AgenticLOCI: A Multi-Agent Memory Framework for Conversational AI with Longitudinal Personalization
paper.abstract: Long-term conversational AI requires two distinct capabilities: remembering what was discussed and adapting to how a user’s preferences evolve over time. We argue these operate on different timescales and require separate but interoperable architectures. AgenticLOCI is a five-agent framework built on this premise: session retrieval fuses a short-term semantic ranker with a long-term keyword scorer via rank fusion, while personalization is maintained through a versioned deliberation-state memory that accumulates decision-episode snapshots across interactions. We evaluate on three benchmarks using Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct. On LoCoMo, the AgenticLOCI Backbone achieves F1 = 0.342 versus BM25 = 0.285 while consuming 7.3\times fewer input tokens per item. On LongMemEval-S, item-level analysis confirms that the two retrieval layers solve architecturally distinct sub-problems; at 7B scale the keyword layer leads, a reversal expected to resolve at larger model sizes where LLM ranking is more reliable. On PersonaMem, all configurations perform within a narrow band, establishing that memory benefit is conditional on context-budget pressure. The longitudinal personalization layer is evaluated on a synthetic mobility benchmark with known user trajectories, keeping 97.6% of stable preference fields unchanged and making warranted updates with 58.3% precision against an ablation baseline. We demonstrate the full framework as a personalized urban mobility assistant for Magdeburg.

paper.title: Capture Is Easy, Forgetting Is Hard: Benchmarking Prospective Memory in Conversational Agents
paper.abstract: Conversational agents are good at recall. But recall only reacts and an agent that answers only what it is asked can never raise what the user never thought to mention. We study the other direction which we call prospective memory. A background agent keeps a small set of pins in the assistant’s context before any question arrives and each pin must be retired by the right authority. A constraint from chat, such as a stolen bike, ends only on the user’s word. One from a city feed, such as a suspended tram line, ends only on the feed’s end message, whatever its forecast said. We release a benchmark of 60 days, ten users and 1,802 graded decisions in a mobility assistant, with automatic answer keys for pinning, forgetting, recommendation and habit discovery. Capture, at least of the templated reveals this benchmark renders, is the easy half. A dense 8B model captures events almost as well as a 397B/17B sparse one and what separates the two is forgetting. The small model hoards and invents. The large model’s one systematic failure is a release cascade, asked to rewrite its whole pin table, it treats any release signal as a reason to shorten it. Asked instead to name its removals as explicit operations, it names only the right ones, every swept pin survives, and required session recall rises from 0.77 to 0.99, from 0.80 to 1.00 on the events both runs captured.

paper.title: When Hiring Becomes Agent-Mediated: Evaluating Access and Recurrence in Two-Agent Résumé Screening
paper.abstract: Hiring is bilateral: employers assess fit, while candidates present and defend evidence of their qualifications. Yet résumé screening—the first gate—is commonly automated as a static, one-call judgment over a résumé–job pair. We study a two-agent alternative in which employer-side and candidate-side agents represent these roles, exchange evidence, and update their judgments before deciding who advances. We compare procedures on 600 constructed résumé–job pairs using GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Two-agent screening advances more applications (33.3% to 39.3% for GPT-5.5; 34.0% to 35.5% for Opus 4.7). Across three runs on the common 191-pair borderline pool, pass-instance rates rise from 4.5% to 26.2% and from 6.5% to 16.1%, respectively. This is not a uniform relaxation: two-agent screening rejects applications one-call advances, changing decisions in both directions. At similar pass volumes, the procedures advance different applications, and no one-call threshold recovers applications consistently selected by two-agent screening. Among discovery-selected cases re-executed in fresh runs, two-agent-only selections recur less often than shared selections—clearly under GPT-5.5, less certainly under Opus 4.7—while a separate one-call follow-up shows no comparable decline. As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the screening procedure—not only the model behind it—shapes who reaches human review and how reliably that access recurs.

paper.title: Research Agents Feed Doubts, Not Beliefs: Auditing Belief Framing in Live-Web Search
paper.abstract: People increasingly hand fact-finding to LLM agents that search the web and return a cited report. We ask whether the belief a user states when making the request changes the research itself. We give 48 expert-verified health claims to four search-equipped agents under believer, skeptic, and neutral framings, analyzing 1,874 of 2,064 registered runs plus second-round arms reported separately. The effect is asymmetric: stating belief leaves conclusions unchanged (0.02, claim-clustered 95% CI -0.04 to 0.09), while stating doubt moves them toward rejection (-0.26, CI -0.39 to -0.15). Across opposing framings the same agent’s conclusion shifts 0.26 points on a five-point scale (CI 0.15 to 0.40), a quarter of one label step, and every system moves the same way. The shift sits on contested claims (0.61) and is small on the settled tiers (0.10 and 0.11). Strictly opposite conclusions were rare and their registered paired test was null (p=0.250), so this is a shift in degree rather than a reversal of verdicts. The trajectories mirror it: skeptic framing more than doubles deny-seeking queries (net -9.9 points against +0.5 for believer framing). Crossing the retrieved evidence between framings splits the gap into how the agent reads what comes back (0.23, CI 0.12 to 0.34) and which evidence comes back at all (0.08, CI 0.00 to 0.16), two channels that add to the end-to-end gap by construction and put about three quarters of it on reading, though the evidence interval reaches zero. Labeling retrieved results against the claim finds no evidence that stated doubt returns a more hostile pool (1.7 points, CI -1.5 to 5.5). An indicative post-hoc follow-up on the 32 claims it reached adds a both-sides instruction to the skeptic condition, where the bias lives, and shifts conclusions by 0.16 (CI 0.04 to 0.30). We release FramedFacts-48: claims, prompts, and analyzed runs.

paper.title: When Failures Propagate: Causal Failure Attribution in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.abstract: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) interleaves retrieval, reasoning, and answer generation across multiple hops. A retrieval error at hop 1 can surface only as a wrong answer at hop 3, while later retrieval can also repair the trajectory. This paper introduces AgenticRAG-FP, an interventional benchmark for causal failure attribution in agentic RAG. The benchmark injects a certified fault at a specified hop, re-executes the downstream trajectory, and evaluates diagnosers against the known intervention site. Its central question is whether a post-hoc trace still identifies the injected hop after the suffix changes. In the dense Claude Haiku 4.5 structural sweep on three-hop MuSiQue questions, coverage-based diagnosis is 0.91 at hop 1 and 0.00 at hops 2 and 3 (n=43, 36, 21 failed trajectories), but it predicts hop 1 in 96% of failures, an earliest-hop rule; at hops 2 and 3, an LLM judge and frozen-hop repair localize only 0.25 to 0.48 of failures. In larger content-corruption runs, depth-2 exact-hop accuracy is 0.00 for coverage, 0.49 for an LLM judge, 0.59 for frozen-hop repair, and 0.14 for suffix regeneration (n=51); the judge and frozen-hop repair do not significantly differ (exact McNemar p=0.33).

paper.title: What Agent Benchmarks Don’t Tell You: Recoverability and Credit Assignment in Agentic Retrieval Evaluation
paper.abstract: Agent quality on long-horizon tasks is usually reported as a single number: the aggregate gain of a tool-using agent over a non-agentic baseline on a benchmark. We argue that this number is not a property of the agent. It is jointly determined by a property of the benchmark and by which sub-component of the agent happens to be load-bearing, and reporting it alone makes agent quality look benchmark-dependent and irreproducible. We propose a four-stage evaluation protocol that separates the two. Stage 1 characterizes the benchmark before any outcome is observed, using an LLM-free diagnostic we call recoverability: whether evidence missed on the first retrieval is still reachable from what the system has already seen, and if so whether it is reachable by reformulation or only by structural navigation. Stage 2 assigns credit with an ablation ladder — one-shot RAG, a choice-free fixed-iterative loop, and a full agent — that localizes any measured gain to iteration or to open-ended agency. Stages 3 and 4 add the validity checks and cost accounting that change verdicts in practice. Applying the protocol to about 6,000 logged agent episodes over eight corpora and three reader families, we find that the headline agent gain ranges from −0.21 to +0.30 (each corpus in its native metric) purely as a function of the recoverability regime, and that on reformulation-recoverable corpora the choice-free loop recovers 65–96% of the gain normally credited to agency under the two stronger readers (and most of it under the open reader). Agency earns its cost only on the longest-horizon, navigation-recoverable corpus, where iteration saturates by round 2 and leaves a residual (+0.15 under the open reader at full N) that no round budget closes under any reader.

paper.title: When the API Speaks the Wrong Language: Revisiting Post-Training for Multilingual Tool Use
paper.abstract: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) for API calling degrades in multilingual settings. A common failure occurs when a model selects the correct tool but generates argument values in an inconsistent language, which we term Argument Language Mismatch (ALM). Although semantically correct, such outputs are operationally invalid and not captured by standard API-calling metrics. We revisit post-training strategies for mitigating ALM and find that, in our benchmark, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a strong baseline, substantially improving argument language consistency and end-to-end function call accuracy. Under consistent model selection, SFT achieves performance comparable to, and sometimes exceeding, more complex reinforcement learning (RL) approaches. We further examine whether RL with structured, argument-aware rewards offers additional benefits. While methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) can improve language consistency and better preserve general reasoning ability, these gains are incremental and most pronounced in generalization and multi-objective trade-offs. Overall, our results suggest that much of the performance in multilingual API grounding can be achieved through careful supervised training, with RL providing fundamental improvements.

paper.title: Beating a Random-Direction Bank Does Not Establish Policy Improvement: An Exact-Value Audit of Activation Steering for Agents
paper.abstract: We audit whether outperforming random activation directions establishes improved agent per- formance. Using Llama-3.1-8B in a molecular identification task, we compute every legal action’s exact probability of eventual success un- der optimal continuation. An entropy-weighted steering direction outperforms all 39 layer- and norm-matched random controls on 42 held-out molecular pools in a frozen comparison. Posthoc audits reveal the limits of this result. An untuned policy that chooses uniformly among legal actions also outperforms every random control, with no detectable difference from the steered policy; uncertainty intervals still admit modest effects in either direction. The steering direction ranks 10th among 36 directions when controls are matched to its construction, and its original-bank rank falls to 3/40 when pools sharing chemical scaffolds are grouped and weighted equally. Executed episodes show no detectable improvement over the unsteered baseline, with both policies performing near random under constrained decoding. These findings concern one model and task; they do not establish that steering cannot improve a competent agent. They demonstrate that su- periority to a random-direction bank does not by itself establish policy improvement. We propose five reporting controls covering trivial baselines, direction construction, inferential units, state selection and horizon, and executed behavior.

paper.title: DySAS: Dynamic State-Aware Student Simulation Beyond Static Personas
paper.abstract: Simulated students play a central role in training and evaluating AI tutor agents, yet most approaches rely on static personas or unconstrained generation and implicitly assume stationary behavior. Real student responses also depend on transient learner states such as affect, attention, and memory that evolve during interaction. We introduce DYSAS, a dynamic state-aware student-simulation framework with three tutoring-facing modules, Affect (A), Attention (T), and Memory (M). Their low, medium, and high levels form the discrete ATM27 state space. We operationalize this interface through Dynamic Learner States (DLS), a prefix-only representation inferred at each turn without future leakage and used to condition student generation. We evaluate static and dynamic variants on the Eedi benchmark across prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and preference optimization. No configuration wins every objective as each of correctness-state match, misconception behavior, social tone, lexical fidelity, and tutor-response compatibility favors different settings. We therefore present DYSAS as an audit mechanism within a multi-objective simulator-selection framework, not as a universally superior add-on.

paper.title: MCPAgentBench: A Real-world Task Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agent MCP Tool Use
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly serving as autonomous agents, and their utilization of external tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is considered a future trend. Current MCP evaluation sets suffer from issues such as reliance on external MCP services and a lack of difficulty awareness. To address these limitations, we propose MCPAgentBench, a benchmark based on real-world MCP definitions designed to evaluate the tool-use capabilities of agents. We construct a dataset containing authentic tasks and simulated MCP tools. The evaluation employs a dynamic sandbox environment that presents agents with candidate tool lists containing distractors, thereby testing their tool selection and discrimination abilities. Furthermore, we introduce comprehensive metrics to measure both task completion rates and execution efficiency. Experiments conducted on state-of-the-art LLMs reveal significant performance differences in handling complex, multi-step tool invocations. All code is open-source at https://github.com/Brunestuder/MCPAgentBench.

paper.title: Grounding First: Auditing a Structured Recovery Wrapper for Local Open-Weight Reflexion Agents
paper.abstract: We audit how action interfaces and recovery mechanisms shape the evaluation of local open-weight Reflexion agents on 134 ALFWorld valid-unseen tasks. The analysis covers six primary admissible-action conditions and historical free-text runs across three model deployments. We organize the audit around four implementation contracts: action execution, recovery triggering, treatment changes, and outcome construction. Historical free-text runs show substantial invalid-output fallback, while designated admissible-parser fallback remains below 1.1 percent; this contrast does not by itself establish parser faithfulness. Structured Recovery Prompting (SRP) combines a recovery prompt with counter resets and relaxed termination limits. Its implementation-reported task-success differences range from 0.00 to +6.72 percentage points and are smaller than the baseline contrast between the two Qwen model sizes. The available evidence supports descriptive comparisons rather than an isolated recovery-prompt effect. The audit identifies incomplete repeat detection and termination-based success labeling, highlighting the importance of trigger coverage and outcome definitions when interpreting recovery results. The contribution is a focused diagnostic audit that connects aggregate performance to implementation behavior and provides concrete checks for evaluating recovery in the studied agents.
