paper.title: What Drives Recovery in Agentic Text-to-Cypher? LAST-CQ: An LLM Agent Self-Refinement Framework
paper.abstract: Agentic pipelines for structured-query generation are rapidly expanding, but it is unclear which part of the loop produces the gain. We use LAST-CQ—a five-agent, training-free, execution-grounded Text-to-Cypher framework—as an instrumented testbed, running three counterfactuals over 2,471 live-database queries and six backbones spanning three vendor scale tiers. Removing correction is worth between 3.1% aggregate execution-BLEU against the single-pass system and 12.3% against a no-refinement counterfactual (up to 80.7% for the weakest backbone). Replacing schema-grounded, LLM-synthesised feedback with raw database error strings costs almost nothing (20.9% vs. 19.9% naive exact match; <0.2% end-to-end; equivalent within ±0.075 set-F1 by two one-sided tests). Spending the same call budget on parallel sampling degrades quality by 10–11%. What works is detecting failure and routing it to a retry, not the feedback sophistication or number of samples. LAST-CQ itself recovers 91.7% of queries that fail under single-pass generation, while a query that succeeds first time still costs exactly one LLM call. We also show that n-gram overlap on serialised results is not a bound in either direction: it over-scores against set equivalence on 65.9% of results while under-scoring against judged semantics. Finally, we calibrate our LLM judge against blind human labels and find it optimistic by 9 points.

paper.title: Runtime Verification of Dimensional Semantics in Checkpointed Large Language Model Tool Workflows
paper.abstract: Tool schemas can validate each language-model-generated call while still allowing quantity identity to disappear during a longer workflow. A model may read 250 milliseconds, checkpoint a bare scalar, and later pass 250 to a destination expecting seconds. We call this loss of executable unit and identity metadata semantic scalarization. We present DIMLOCK, a small runtime that carries quantities as opaque references, resolves exact compatible conversions, and rejects cross-dimensional references before destination execution. We also introduce a frozen stress protocol with logical checkpoint save/load, same- and cross- dimension distractors, and receipt-backed scoring. Across 36 workflows and 540 controlled fault trials, DIMLOCK contains all 108 primary faults while prose and structured scalar handoffs contain none. A same- dimension identity swap defeats every interface, confirming the boundary of dimension-only enforcement. Native MCP pilots cover 216 Codex trajectories and a balanced 36-trajectory Claude Sonnet replication; tested models usually rejected explicit traps, so we make no prevalence claim. The result is a focused runtime invariant and a reproducible test for a failure class that local tool schemas do not express.

paper.title: Bayesian Belief Layer for Controllable Opinion Dynamics in LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Toronto Metropolitan University, Havergal College, Toronto Metropolitan University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Canadian Science Publishing, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Flybits Inc. and Toronto Metropolitan University

paper.abstract: LLM agents in social simulation revise their opinions implicitly, in context: how open an agent is to persuasion can neither be specified nor verified, and collective outcomes inherit the model’s training prior. We introduce Bayesian Chronicle Agents (BCA), a minimal belief layer separating what an agent believes from how it speaks. Each stance is a probability, updated by one Bayesian step per utterance heard. A single prior-strength parameter \kappa encodes stubbornness, modeled after its role in Friedkin–Johnsen (FJ) opinion dynamics. We then sweep this parameter to yield three canonical regimes of opinion dynamics on demand (consensus, persistent disagreement, committed-minority influence), with persistent disagreement matching the FJ closed-form fixed points at R^2 = 0.93–0.99. We further show that prescribed \kappa remains recoverable after the language round-trip, with perfect rank-order recovery across all four models. Explicit belief also makes simulation auditable: the layer surfaces systematic per-model stance biases that end-to-end simulation would silently absorb.

paper.title: Failing Agents Leave Traces: Telemetry Signatures for Multi-Tier Agent Evaluation
paper.abstract: Agent evaluation today depends on per-trace LLM-judge inference or human review, too expensive to run on every trace; production systems fall back to sampling a fraction. We find that failing agents leave a detectable behavioral signature in standard observability telemetry: disproportionate effort relative to outcome. We formalize four behavioral failure signatures from agent telemetry, validated on 4,671 traces spanning five agent domains: Compensatory Effort (17–159% more effort on each domain’s primary signal, all five domains, p<0.006, the dominant signature every- where tested); Output Inflation (+38% larger patches on SWE-rebench; direction and reliability vary by domain); Unfocused Orchestra- tion (+5.98–12.3% higher token entropy, four of five domains); and Correlation Decoupling (effort-signal correlations shift structurally between pass and fail traces, p<0.001, three domains). A simple threshold check over these signals, with no judge, no label, and no model call, already catches 52.9–61.5% of failures. Across three human-labeled benchmarks, judges miss 6.5–18.1% of confirmed failures on the two directly comparable ones, and a trained telemetry classifier (AUROC 0.821) recovers 61.5–75.4% of each judge’s misses; combining judge and classifier cuts the miss rate from 18.1% to 4.4%, a 4.1× reduction against the weakest of the eight judges tested (GPT-4o-mini); stronger judges start with fewer misses, so the reduction is correspondingly smaller.

paper.title: EARS: Explanatory Abstention for Reliable Sub-Agent Modeling in Large-Scale Multi-Agent Systems
paper.abstract: In large-scale enterprise settings, centralized multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly adopted, in which a coordinator delegates user requests to lightweight, domain-specialized sub-agents. While this architecture improves modularity, scalability, and cost efficiency, its reliability depends not only on accurate routing but also on sub-agents’ ability to calibrate their responses to capability constraints. In particular, sub-agents built on smaller fine-tuned models often struggle with such calibration, leading them to over-answer ambiguous, underspecified, misrouted, or unsupported requests and produce hallucinated outputs instead of actionable feedback. To address this challenge, we present EARS (Explanatory Abstention for Reliable Sub-Agent Modeling), a production-oriented framework that reframes sub-agent abstention as an inter-agent communication protocol: a sub-agent does not merely abstain, but exposes an actionable failure state to the coordinator. EARS curates human-agent interaction data using an ensemble of calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge models, producing structured abstention labels and rationales under a taxonomy of sub-agent failure modes. These data are used to fine-tune sub-agents to detect failure conditions and return rationales for coordinator-level clarification, rerouting, or fallback. We evaluate EARS in a large-scale production e-commerce assistant supporting enterprise business intelligence workflows. EARS improves the overall response pass rate from 68.5% to 78.9%, demonstrating that sub-agent-side explanatory abstention improves MAS reliability.

paper.title: ExGQL: Self-Improving Natural Language-to-Graph Query Generation via Experience-Guided Learning
paper.abstract: Natural language-to-graph query generation (NL2GQL) requires schema-aware reasoning and multi-hop traversal planning, posing graph-specific challenges beyond the extensively studied Text-to-SQL setting. Existing NL2GQL systems typically solve each query in isolation, limiting their ability to learn from prior executions. We present ExGQL, an experience-guided framework for self-improving NL2GQL. ExGQL combines hierarchical memory, experience evolution, and capability synthesis to distill execution feedback into reusable reasoning strategies and convert validated strategies into executable capabilities. We further introduce a Failure-Directed Curriculum (FDC) for a separate practice phase, in which recurring failure patterns guide the selection of tasks that address the system’s current weaknesses. We evaluate ExGQL on NL2GQL-Bench, a benchmark of 400 expert-annotated graph query tasks over a production-scale graph database. ExGQL achieves an average accuracy of 0.869 versus 0.662 for the strongest evaluated baseline (+31% relative improvement), while reducing average query-generation time by 28%. In a separate practice phase, FDC reaches comparable accuracy of 0.861 with 60% fewer practice episodes and 36% lower runtime than fixed-order practice. These results show that NL2GQL systems can improve by reusing execution-derived experience, while failure-directed practice makes experience acquisition more efficient.

paper.title: Environment Steering: Using Data Flow Control to Improve Agent Utility and Safety

author.affiliation: State University of New York at Buffalo

paper.abstract: LLM agents can make unsafe tool calls even when instructed to behave safely. Existing defenses constrain agents before execution, modify tool inputs/outputs, or rely on LLM judges; these approaches may depend on model behavior or block unsafe actions without helping the agent recover. We argue that the execution environment should instead enforce safety as the agent runs and steer it toward safe alternatives when violations occur—we call this \textbf{Environment Steering}. We implement this by modeling the agent and harness execution state as database tables, track the record-level data flows, and check these data flows against declarative policies during runtime. When violations are detected, policy- and context-specific feedback steers the agent toward safe trajectories. On AgentDyn, this enables the agent to improve task success rate over no-defense while achieving 0% attack success rate.

paper.title: Role-Diverse Agent Forests for Neuroimaging Triage: When Does Prompt-Induced Role Diversity Help?

author.affiliation: St.Cyril and Methodius University and ITQuarks

paper.abstract: Majority-vote LLM ensembles improve accuracy monotonically with ensemble size when agents are homogeneous samples of the same prompt (Li et al., 2024). We test whether this holds for four heterogeneous clinical-role prompts on one frozen MedGemma backbone, across binary tumor detection, tumor subtyping, MS, and stroke triage. Our comparison is against single-agent triage: we ask whether role-diverse voting clears that bar, not whether it matches sampling diversity, since we do not run a paired homogeneous-sampling forest. On a paired 500-image evaluation per task, a four-agent forest does not reliably beat single-agent triage: significantly worse on binary tumor (both stages) and MS end-to-end, indistinguishable on tumor subtyping and stroke. Pairwise error correlation between roles is far from independent on every task (φ = 0.43–0.75 vs. φ = 0 under independence), explaining why voting fails to average errors out. Roles diverge behaviorally on the easiest task but collapse onto a shared “normal” bias on the two hardest, so voting cannot recover sensitivity no member has. Dissent rate, a candidate escalation signal, is valid on two tasks, uninformative on MS, and inverted on stroke, where agreement is less reliable than disagreement. These results argue against assuming role diversity on a shared backbone helps by default, and for task-conditional validation before deployment.

paper.title: The Audit Decides the Verdict: Instrument Effects Rival Demographic Bias in LLM Decision Audits
paper.abstract: Whether a language model looks demographically biased can depend on how the audit asks its question. A charitable-aid benchmark reports that the same models favor minority applicants when rating requests one at a time and penalize some when ranking side by side. We test whether that reversal generalizes to hiring, lending, and medical triage: 40,726 requests to five models, applications differing only in the applicant’s name, and a primary test fixed before collection. It does not. None of 36 planned contrasts survives correction. The rating advantage keeps its sign at roughly half the published size, and a precision extension bounds any hiring ranking penalty below the published effect, though the lending and triage ranking floors sit above that margin, so the exclusion is conclusive for hiring ranking and for rating in all three domains only. Planted disparities tracking their injected sizes and a directional replication on the original aid materials bound these nulls. The audit is livelier than the demographics: models recognize transparent audits nearly always, tie every identical-content comparison whether the varying detail is race or a hobby, and reward first-listed candidates as much as any demographic effect we measure. Audit verdicts reflect audit construction more than demographic bias.

paper.title: SEDIMA: Cross-Run Hierarchical Insight Memory for Evolutionary Search Agents
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven evolutionary search is a powerful paradigm for automated program and algorithm discovery, yet existing systems are largely memoryless: each run explores from scratch, so agents repeatedly rediscover the same improvements and re-encounter the same dead ends. We introduce SEDIMA, a persistent hierarchical insight memory for evolutionary search agents. SEDIMA distills raw traces into natural-language insights, clusters them by semantic similarity using attention-weighted centroids, and retrieves relevant guidance to condition future mutations, accumulating transferable knowledge across runs and problems rather than within a single trajectory. As a drop-in module that leaves the search operators unmodified, SEDIMA improves average final performance by 5.5% on AlgoTune and 6.6% on ALE-Bench LITE under a fixed budget of 100 evaluated candidates. Under OpenEvolve, SEDIMA requires 32.3% fewer iterations on average to reach baseline-best performance across the five evaluated backbones.

paper.title: When Critics Go Stale: Benchmarking Safety Guardrail Degradation Under Environment Drift
paper.abstract: LLM-based critics are widely deployed as safety guardrails for agentic systems, yet their reliability under realistic operating conditions remains underexplored. We demonstrate that critics calibrated against a fixed system snapshot degrade as tools are added and application domains expand, with no external signal indicating weakened detection capability. We formalize this problem along controlled axes and introduce DRIFT (Detecting Reliability Issues From Tool-scaling), a benchmark for measuring critic robustness under environment change. Building on SafeToolBench’s multi-domain tool ecosystem, we construct verified cross-app composition scenarios, both violating and compliant, where policy violations emerge only from data flow across application boundaries, and evaluate 9 models across 6 provider families on a two-dimensional scaling matrix separating intra-app noise from cross-app noise. We find that (1) all 9 models degrade under cross-app scaling, with UPR increases ranging from +0.083 to +0.296, (2) tool scaling shifts critics toward reduced discriminability, missed violations rise while false blocks simultaneously fall, and (3) cross-app noise consistently dominates intra-app noise, with cross-app deltas positive for all nine models (sign test p = 0.004) while intra-app deltas are directionless (4 of 9 positive, p = 1.0). DRIFT provides a controlled methodology for measuring critic robustness as tool ecosystems evolve, and our results argue for monitoring UPR and FBR jointly rather than aggregate accuracy alone.

paper.title: Are LLM Shopping Agents Behaviorally Distinguishable from Human Shoppers? A Session-Level Study
paper.abstract: Large language models can now operate a web browser and carry out multi-step shopping tasks. Does such an agent leave a behavioral signature in a session that separates it from a person, even when it drives a real browser and presents an ordinary client fingerprint? We study the question at the session level. We first show that weak per-action evidence aggregates into a session-level distinction whose error decays exponentially in the number of actions. We then define six families of behavioral signals, each grounded in a documented difference between goal-directed automation and human browsing, and combine them in a classifier we call HABITS (Human–Agent Behavioral Invariants from Traffic at Session-level). Labeled agent sessions are scarce, so we describe a simulation methodology for driving language models through shopping tasks and instantiate it on public data with realism-controlled planner agents. We evaluate on five public benchmarks spanning e-commerce clickstreams, web-task demonstrations, and mouse dynamics, reimplementing prior methods on the identical corpus. Against agents that imitate human timing, timing-only classifiers fall to 0.35 recall at a 1% false-positive rate and to 0.01 -0.02 when timing is fully matched, while HABITS reaches 0.96 on the clickstream corpus. Paired tests separate HABITS from every restricted-view baseline, and equivalence tests show that strong classifiers given the same features are interchangeable, which places the contribution in the behavioral view rather than the estimator. A check against real agent trajectories supports the structural assumption our simulator relies on and finds one realism parameter set too favorably.

paper.title: BioSciReview-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Silent Scientific Bug Detection in Bioinformatics Code
paper.abstract: Existing coding-agent benchmarks test functional correctness—whether code runs and returns expected outputs. Silent scientific methodology bugs pose a different challenge: they execute without error yet produce plausible, scientifically wrong results. We introduce BioSciReview-Bench, a benchmark of 200 manually reviewed synthetic bioinformatics code snippets (100 matched correct–buggy pairs) spanning five domains and six bug categories. Each snippet is presented in isolation without construction metadata; agents must detect whether a bug exists, localize it to a specific displayed line, and classify it by type. We evaluate six configurations across three model families and two agent harnesses. All achieve detection F1 of 0.94–0.99, but performance drops with stricter requirements: joint localization within three lines reaches 0.92–0.98 F1, and full diagnosis requiring exact line plus correct category falls to 0.74–0.89 F1, a gap of approximately 10–23 percentage points below detection. Filtering and quality-control bugs have the lowest average Full Diagnosis@±3 success rate, and agents sometimes confuse them with normalization errors. Detection performance is high on this controlled benchmark, while delivering actionable diagnoses remains substantially harder.

paper.title: Do Tool Schemas Fully Specify Argument Binding?
paper.abstract: Tool schemas constrain the structure of a call but need not determine how request evidence becomes argument values. We formalize this layer as a field-level binding contract over presence, evidence, ordered operations, parameters, and validation, and state an identifiability boundary: no schema-only estimator can guarantee recovery of policy distinctions absent from its input. We audit all 1,311 filtered requests in pinned Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) V4 Live Simple and Multiple with five open checkpoints and the official abstract-syntax-tree (AST) checker. A partial structural diagnostic and AST acceptance are non-nested: 1,470 of 6,555 calls pass only the diagnostic and 50 pass only AST. A stratified AI-only audit finds coarse concern detection far more consistent across two isolated passes than fine attribution. A pre-specified test of a deterministic schema-derived operation-label encoding gives 67.70% AST acceptance versus 68.27% under the same guidance without field tags (-0.56 points; 95% task-cluster CI -1.17 to +0.05; 186 fixes, 223 breaks). Value-only turnover is nearly balanced; the net imbalance sits in key-set changes. The point estimate reverses sign on one post-hoc out-of-panel checkpoint; thus no improvement is established on the fixed panel, and independently authored contracts remain untested.

paper.title: Testing Behavioral Adaptation in Repeated Interactions Between LLM Agents
paper.abstract: High aggregate scores can make language agents appear socially responsive even when they merely repeat a prompt-conditioned action. We introduce an identifiability-first framework that separates observed outcomes from evidence of adaptation. Across 3,465 released iterated-prisoner’s-dilemma simulations, 94.5% never change joint regime, leaving reciprocity largely unidentifiable. Controlled histories across nine models reveal opponent-dependent responses that vary substantially across equivalent interfaces. The released checkpoints have the smallest opponent-recency effects. Only the intervention cohort shows reliable propagation after a scripted defection. The diagnostic transfers to longer histories, a multiplayer game, and released-interface wrappers, although model rankings do not. Outcome-only evaluation conflates regime selection with adaptive behavior. Separating opportunity, response, and robustness prevents stable outcomes from being mistaken for social dynamics.

paper.title: CaseInterviewBench: Evaluating Agentic AI’s Purpose-Reflective Autonomy to Uncover What the User Really Needs

author.affiliation: Strategic Digital Business Unit, Mamezou CO., Ltd.

paper.abstract: Agentic autonomy is essential for large language models (LLMs) to function as agentic AI systems, yet existing benchmarks often emphasize operational aspects, or HOW an agent behaves, such as tool use. The ability to reconsider the user’s underlying purpose, or WHY the agent acts, remains underexplored. We define this capability as "purpose-reflective autonomy" and introduce CaseInterviewBench, an interactive, interview-style benchmark inspired by consultant recruitment. The benchmark contains 104 predefined scenarios, each with public background context, an initial request, hidden facts, and ground-truth problem formulations and resolutions. The target LLM asks questions to uncover hidden facts, then identifies the actual problem and proposes a resolution, enabling us to observe how it infers, revises, and refines its understanding of the scenario’s underlying purpose in a structured setting. We evaluate hidden-fact disclosure, final problem formulation, and resolution using rule-based metrics and LLM-as-a-judge assessments. Across several frontier and open-weight models, we found substantial room for improvement. We also observed severe violations in which some models fabricated facilitator responses during the benchmark flow, potentially creating serious risks in agentic execution.

paper.title: A Case Study of On-Premise ReAct for Collaborative Robot Programming
paper.abstract: LLM-based coding agents are increasingly used in software development, but their use in industrial robot programming remains constrained by vendor-specific APIs, organization-specific code assets, and on-premise deployment requirements. We study a bounded ReAct agent that uses local retrieval over API documentation and code examples to generate collaborative-robot programs from natural-language requirements.This work is a case study of a structured programming domain in which domain knowledge must remain within the organizational boundary and local models may be sufficient. We evaluate seven open-weight models from 7B to 32B parameters, with five independent runs per model, and include one commercial model as a reference. We also apply the same framework to a smaller public Universal Robots set.Under our agent and evaluation setup, the strongest local 27B model achieves a mean task success rate of 89.6%. Smaller models often use more steps and tokens because they repeat retrieval or fail to convert retrieved evidence into code. These results suggest that model selection should consider task success, interaction efficiency, and run-to-run consistency.

paper.title: Causal Episodic Memory for Feedback-Driven Agent Repair

author.affiliation: Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology
Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology

paper.abstract: LLM agents that repair failures often discard successful corrections, forcing later episodes to rediscover similar solutions. We study whether finalized repair outcomes can improve subsequent Text-to-SQL episodes without parameter updates. We introduce MERIT, a training-free agent that maintains an online dual-polarity memory of oracle-verified corrections and observed unsuccessful directions. Under oracle-assisted benchmark feedback, only memories from earlier finalized episodes are eligible for retrieval. A deterministic classifier assigns a coarse failure type, which conditions a hybrid lexical-dense retriever before the frozen model generates each revision. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with identical initial predictions and repair budgets, MERIT improves execution accuracy over stateless iterative repair from 66.34% to 69.79% on Spider and from 47.35% to 48.44% on BIRD. Paired analyses provide clear evidence for the Spider gain but weaker evidence on BIRD. MERIT is not reliably separated from untyped dynamic retrieval on either benchmark, while Reflexion-style memory reaches 51.24% on BIRD at substantially higher inference cost. Ablations show that negative memory contributes modestly, the value of type conditioning and lexical-dense ranking is dataset dependent, and schema-local experience provides the most consistent benefit. These results clarify when causal cross-query memory improves repair and when broader memory representations remain preferable. Our implementation is available here: https://github.com/nhatkhangcs/merit

paper.title: Chronicle: Cut-Point Replay for Regression Testing of LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Birla Institute of Technology and Science

paper.abstract: Large language model responses are non-deterministic, so failures in LLM agents are hard to reproduce: a failure depends on inference that is not bitwise reproducible, on tools that read changing state, and on a multi-step trajectory that a re-run rarely repeats. Record-and-replay makes a run reproducible, but existing agent tooling records runs only to trace or score them, not to test a code change against them. We present Chronicle, which records an agent run at its non-deterministic boundaries as immutable envelopes and replays it from the record. Its central operation, cut-point replay, serves a chosen subset of boundaries from the record and executes the complementary subset live with new code, turning a recorded incident into a regression test that runs in continuous integration. On a benchmark of 6 recorded failures with simulated model boundaries, recording adds 23 μs per crossing (0.008% of an assumed 300 ms model call), full replay issues zero model calls and is bit-stable across 20 repetitions, and cut-point tests fail on faulty code and pass on guarded and benign changes for all 6 incidents. In a mutation study of the guarded tools, cut-point tests catch every mutant that lets the recorded unsafe action through, while a baseline that stubs every boundary, using the same assertion, catches none. Chronicle and the benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/theagentplane/chronicle.

paper.title: Contract Before Code: Failure-Compiled Contracts for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
paper.abstract: Long-horizon coding agents can make many edits before testing a task-wide assumption about an API, authentication mode, environment, or persistent state. A late verifier then exposes that the implementation rests on a false premise. We call the missing step contract acquisition and propose Contract Before Code (CBC), harness-level middleware that compiles historical failures into executable preflight gates. CBC normalizes trajectories, extracts recurring failure signatures, and compiles contracts containing an applicability condition, a probe template, and a planning consequence. At inference time, it retrieves applicable contracts and runs instantiated probes before broad implementation work. Among 1,421 parsed failed SWE-Marathon trajectories, weak labels identify candidate rates of 2.6% overall and 17.5% on stripe-clone; these are not root-cause prevalence estimates. A 120-trajectory human audit reports 76.3% contract precision and 71.4% executable-probe synthesis. Across four service/API-clone tasks and 32 runs per method, CBC achieves 31.3% success (95% CI 18.0–48.6), an observed 21.9-percentage-point increase over vanilla, with 55.6% fewer pre-verification edits at 1.11× normalized token cost. The small end-to-end study supports preliminary within-family benefits; broader transfer and the stability of these gains remain unestablished.

paper.title: DeepRewind: Predicting and Repairing Premature Commitments in Deep Research Agents
paper.abstract: Deep-research agents conduct long-horizon investigations through iterative search, evidence evaluation, belief revision, and synthesis. However, they may commit to claims before sufficient evidence is available, causing later reasoning to reinforce an incorrect interpretation. We introduce DeepRewind, an additive control layer for reversible deep research that represents the agent’s evolving epistemic state as a typed graph of sources, evidence, claims, hypotheses, assumptions, commitments, plans, and drafts. Before accepting an intermediate conclusion, a prompt-based world model predicts its impact and estimates reversibility based on hypothesis narrowing, information loss, recovery cost, and contradiction-trigger coverage. A binary controller blocks risky commitments, while a consistency monitor performs dependency-aware rollback when later evidence invalidates them. Across DRBench and LiveDRBench, DeepRewind improves insight recall by 3.6 percentage points and reduces premature commitments by 59.1% relative to Open Deep Research.

paper.title: BirdsongChat: A Hybrid Multi-Agent Framework for Interactive Multimodal Embodied Behavior Simulation
paper.abstract: Multimodal embodied systems require translating human intentions into interpretable and coordinated behaviors across heterogeneous modalities. However, existing multimodal agents often rely on implicit representations, limiting controllability and cross-modal consistency. We present a hybrid multi-agent framework for interactive multimodal behavior simulation that bridges semantic reasoning and physical execution through a Unified Parameter Representation (UPR). LLM-based reasoning agents transform multimodal inputs into UPR, which encodes behavioral states and interpretable control parameters for simulation agents generating synchronized 3D motion, spatialized soundscapes, and environmental behaviors. We develop BirdsongChat as a prototype implementation of the proposed framework, using interactive avian behavior simulation as a testbed that tightly couples motion, vocalization, and environmental context. BirdsongChat is evaluated on text- and image-guided scenarios involving species, behaviors, affective states, environments, and multi-bird interactions. The system achieves normalized scores of 94.4% for cross-modal coherence, 100% for affective consistency, and 92.6% for generation consistency. These results demonstrate that an explicit intermediate representation effectively bridges semantic reasoning and physical execution, improving controllability and multimodal synchronization. The proposed framework thus offers a generalizable design principle for embodied AI systems requiring interpretable semantic-to-physical coordination across modalities, with potential applications in bio-inspired ecoacoustics, swarm robotics, virtual environments, and creative multimedia.

paper.title: An Evaluation of Data Leakage Risks in Tool-Using LLM Agents in Realistic Scenarios
paper.abstract: AI agents are increasingly being adopted in enterprise and personal settings with access to emails, databases, documents, and other tools where they can read, update, and disseminate sensitive information. Much of prior research on data leakage risks in agents has focused on adversarial data exfiltration through prompt injections and jailbreaks. However, sensitive information may also be exposed during non-adversarial use, thereby creating leakage risks even when users issue benign requests. We report a joint evaluation by the Singapore AI Safety Institute and the Korea AI Safety Institute examining agent data leakage in 12 realistic, non-adversarial tasks, spanning areas like customer support, DevOps, web automation, and enterprise and personal productivity, covering five risk types: lack of data awareness, audience awareness, policy compliance, data minimization, and access-boundary awareness. Both institutes tested a common set of scenarios mirroring real-world deployments. To do so, they implemented independent testing pipelines with ReAct-style agent scaffolds, model-simulated users, MCP-based tool environments, and task-specific LLM-judge rubrics. Across the three tested agents, none achieved fully correct and fully safe execution across all scenarios. Successful task completion often coincided with data-handling failures like accessing unnecessary information or disclosing information to inappropriate recipients, indicating that capability and data-handling safety should be evaluated separately. Qualitative review also revealed claim-action mismatches, simulation-aware behavior, user-simulator role reversal, and interpretation gaps in automated judging. Overall, the results indicate that operational data leakage is a first-order agent-safety concern distinct from adversarial exfiltration. This work also provides a methodology for future evaluations and highlights good practices in agentic testing including creating realistic test environments, LLM-simulated human users, and granular evaluation criteria to improve LLM-judge performance.

paper.title: GLOBE: Evolving Structured Agentic Memory for E-commerce Product Optimization in Generative Search
paper.abstract: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.

paper.title: COMPASS: Critique-guided Optimization of MetaPolicies for Agentic Systems with Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: University of Colorado at Boulder and Google

paper.abstract: As large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, optimizing their behavior in agentic reasoning and tool-use environments remains challenging due to the stochasticity of environment trajectories and associated high reward latencies. Existing automated prompt optimization (APO) paradigms struggle in these regimes: discrete evolutionary methods (e.g., GEPA, ACE) lack parametric memory, while instance-level reinforcement learning (RL) approaches suffer from severe gradient variance and reward collapse on small, human-curated datasets. To address these limitations, we introduce COMPASS (Critique-guided Optimization of MetaPolicies for Agentic SystemS), a sample-efficient dual-agent framework that shifts optimization toward task-level metapolicies and demonstrates that an RL-based prompter policy can be effectively trained on such tasks. To overcome sparse feedback, COMPASS introduces a Critique Experience Buffer that couples scalar rewards with dense textual critiques. This mechanism allows an active “Prompter” policy to internalize corrective linguistic patterns and amortize experiential self-reflection directly into its weights. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that COMPASS stabilizes training and yields up to 2.4\times faster convergence. On complex reasoning (BBEH) and tool-use (\tau-bench) benchmarks, our framework improves success rates from 55% to 90% and 74% to 91%, respectively, while naturally discovering specialized algorithmic strategies.

paper.title: From Trajectories to Workflows: Online Procedural Memory Abstraction for Language Agents

author.affiliation: Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.

paper.abstract: Procedural memory for language agents typically accumulates as trajectories, scripts, or task-specific skills, so memory grows with the number of interactions rather than the number of distinct procedures learned. We propose a workflow-centric procedural memory framework that continually consolidates repeated experience into a bounded set of natural-language workflows. These workflows are merged online under outcome-conditioned update policies. On ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, our memory is competitive with trajectory-level procedural memory on task success while using 3.5\times fewer memory tokens on average (1.1-9.1\times across settings), showing that representation besides construction, retrieval and updating is also a key design axis for scalable procedural memory.

paper.title: Prior-History Sensitivity in Agentic Safety Evaluations
paper.abstract: Stateful agents increasingly leverage execution logs, tool outputs, feedback, and summaries from prior interactions to inform future behavior. Despite this, safety evaluations typically evaluate agents using either a singular fixed prior history or an empty baseline, via a uniform history rendering. We argue that such evaluations only illustrate a conditional snapshot of model behavior and fail to demonstrate whether these conclusions generalize across plausible prior histories and history renderings. We use the Inspect Evals agentic misalignment benchmark, finding that among eight benign prior histories, a single Opus 4.1 history significantly and repeatedly increased harmful-action rates, whereas the remaining seven alternatives exhibited no such increase relative to the empty history condition. While additional rollout replications improved statistical confidence, they did not improve the representativeness of the overall sample. Conversely, all eight Qwen3-30B histories resulted in an average decrease of 26.3 percentage points in observed harmful actions. Furthermore, we examined four distinct history renderings of 15 benign prior histories across 900 Opus blackmail rollouts. History renderings with tool results and neutral summaries reduced mean harmful-action rates by 10.0 and 15.0 percentage points, respectively. These results emphasize the necessity for evaluations to incorporate diverse, plausible prior histories and history renderings to establish that their findings generalize.

paper.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
paper.abstract: Modern LLM coding agents—Claude Code, OpenHands—share a common inefficiency: they spend most of their token budget finding the file to patch, not patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, dominated by grep, glob, and view_file calls. No open, systematically-studied agent-style code retriever exists at scale to shorten this phase. We introduce CodeGrep, a 14B retrieval agent trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep/glob/read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent.On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep preserves the downstream resolve rate (25.8% → 27.0%, +1.2pp) while delivering a much larger efficiency gain (−15% rounds, −19% tokens on resolved instances). Across three retrievers, downstream utility follows a precision threshold: BM25 (precision 0.375) degrades the agent, Jina (0.445) is neutral, and only CodeGrep (0.677) crosses the threshold at which retrieval begins to buy efficiency. To enable this study, we mine supervision from 67K open-source agent trajectories (CATM) and build a Git-worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL. In our setting, applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer, rather than the reward layer, holds KL drift to one-third and translates cleanly into downstream efficiency. We will release the model, training pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses.

paper.title: SkillCombiner: Optimizing Agent Skills via Edit Combination Search

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology

paper.abstract: Large language model agents are often guided by reusable natural-language skills that provide task-specific instructions. Existing work automatically refines these skills by using LLMs to propose and repeatedly incorporate textual edits from agent feedback. We find that the resulting performance depends substantially on which proposed edits are combined, and adding an edit can even degrade the skill. We therefore introduce SkillCombiner, which generates candidate edits and explicitly searches over their combinations. Across various settings, SkillCombiner matches or exceeds a strong baseline in mean performance while reducing optimizer cost by 75.2% and total optimization-stage cost by 21.5% on average. These results show that edit combination is an important optimization target in agent skill refinement.

paper.title: When Better Turns Do Not Make Better Agents: Diagnosing the Gap Between Next-Turn Metrics and Workflow Success
paper.abstract: Agent models are frequently evaluated one decision at a time, where the model predicts the next action based on the gold interaction history, which is scored against a reference. We investigate whether improvement under this protocol is predictive of improved autonomous workflow execution. We study pre-SFT and supervised fine-tuned (SFT) Qwen3 models at 4B and 14B parameters and Gemma 3 models at 4B and 12B parameters on multi-turn customer-support workflows. We find that SFT consistently improves text-turn success, and that overall next-turn success increases for every model under gold-history evaluation. However, these improvements do not transfer to autonomous workflow execution. Tool-specific gains also vary across metrics and models. None of the four SFT models succeeds under holistic workflow evaluation, with strict trajectory completion reaching at most 10.4% workflow success. Our results show that next-turn evaluation is not a reliable proxy for workflow success, motivating separate reporting of text quality, local action correctness, tool execution, and end-to-end task completion.

paper.title: Dynamics-Aware Navigation for Autonomous UI Agents on Directional-Input Devices
paper.abstract: Autonomous GUI agents have achieved near-perfect task completion on touchscreen benchmarks by tapping directly at target coordinates. However, smart televisions, game consoles, and set-top boxes require users to navigate with a directional pad (D-PAD), turning element selection into a planning problem over an unknown focus-transition graph. We study autonomous task completion on streaming TV devices, where an agent navigates 68 streaming applications using only D-PAD inputs to perform four tasks: login, reaching subscription plans, content search, and settings navigation. We formalize this setting as a partially observable Markov decision process and compare two architectures using three open-weight vision-language models (Google Gemma 3 at 4B and 27B parameters, and Alibaba Qwen3-VL at 235B): (i) a VLM that maps screenshots directly to D-PAD actions, following the paradigm that dominates current benchmarks, and (ii) a system that maintains an explicit model of focus transition dynamics via Bayesian belief updates and graph-based path planning. The dynamics-aware system improves login success for every model tested, by a mean of 8.8 percentage points, and for the Gemma models its relative advantage widens on tasks requiring extended navigation. The benefit is inverse to model scale, ranging from 16.2 points for the 4B model to 2.9 points for the 235B model. A 4B model with dynamics awareness (32.4%) outperforms a 27B model without it (26.5%), indicating that transition knowledge can outweigh a 6.75×increase in model parameters.

paper.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
paper.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models’ ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.

paper.title: Diversity and Deliberation in Homogeneous LLM Prediction Polls
paper.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems increasingly combine model-generated judgments for forecasting and collective decision-making. However, homogeneous agent systems, i.e., those that share a model and evidence, may produce correlated forecasts, and communication may further contract the diversity that remains. We examine these issues in live LLM prediction polls. Across 189 resolved snapshots, mean residual-error correlation was 0.910. Semantic prompt differences were associated with forecast differences, but diversity-aware selection did not detectably outperform prespecified random ensembles. Standard deliberation removed approximately twice as much disagreement benefit as it added through improvements in individual forecasts at the point estimates, with no detectable improvement in aggregate accuracy. In a prospective intervention, a probability-blind summary of forecast-relevant claims retained 93% of initial dispersion, compared with 29% under standard exchange.

paper.title: When Agreement Is Not Enough: Evidence-Risk Arbitration for Multi-Strategy Agentic QA
paper.abstract: Multi-strategy question-answering agents often produce several plausible responses to one query, but must ultimately show the user only one. Voting treats answer agreement as trust, yet strategies can disagree for different reasons, and identical answers can rest on evidence of unequal quality. We cast this final choice as diagnosis-first evidence-risk arbitration and introduce the Evidence-Risk-Aware Strategy Reranker (ERSR), which canonicalizes a pool of six responses, classifies their agreement type, and applies a type-specific evidence rule while returning one unchanged response. Calibration uses only development data; for each evaluation item, trusted reference answers, trusted reference evidence, and utility stay hidden, and the selector never abstains. On a 900-item development split drawn from FEVER, HotpotQA, and SciFact, ERSR improves evidence-aware utility over a development-selected fixed strategy by +0.052, with the largest gains on label conflicts and unanimous answers with uneven evidence. These results suggest that response-set structure, not agreement alone, is a useful signal for choosing trustworthy answers.

paper.title: FlexSciEval: Structure-Grounded Multi-agent Evaluation for Flexible Electronics Research

author.affiliation: Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology and Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Evaluating research in flexible electronics requires weighing evidence across multiple technical and manufacturing dimensions. However, current LLM-based approaches largely rely on unstructured text and generic evaluation criteria, limiting their ability to assess scientific work at the device level. We present FlexSciEval, a multi-agent framework that first turns each paper or research plan into an auditable structured record, then uses dimension-specific agents to score academic impact, fabrication realizability, and novelty. We also construct a 60-paper expert-annotated benchmark for validation and scale the framework to 4,158 papers. FlexSciEval reduces overall mean absolute error by 10.4% compared with direct LLM evaluation on the benchmark annotated by experts, although gains vary by model and dimension. These results indicate that grounding LLM evaluation in structured and dimension-specific evidence improves the reliability of automated scientific assessment in the field of flexible electronics, providing a practical basis for more reliable agent-based evaluation in experimental device research in the future.

paper.title: What People Almost Did: Evaluating LLM Social Simulations Beyond Behavioral Fit
paper.abstract: LLM-based social simulations are primarily evaluated for behavioral fit, testing whether agents reproduce the actions or response distributions of the people they are simulating. However, the promise of simulation extends beyond behavioral fit. Simulations can explain human behavior, diagnose barriers, and compare large-scale interventions. These use cases depend on understanding \textit{why} people acted a certain way, not just \textit{what} they did. As a result, behavioral fit is insufficient for these types of claims because behavior underdetermines the reasoning process behind it. For instance, the behavior of staying silent may be due to disinterest or suppressed speech, and not answering a call may be due to distrust of the caller or limited phone access. In this paper, we propose \textit{representational adequacy} as a new evaluation target for LLM-based social simulations. By leveraging LLM reasoning traces, representational adequacy measures whether a simulation’s scenario–reasoning–action triples preserve the reasoning process behind the behavior in a way that is faithful to the population and scenarios being simulated. We distinguish representational adequacy from interpretability and alignment metrics, propose ways to integrate it into simulation research, and pose its measurement as an open problem.

paper.title: Lost in the Handoff: Contract-Aware Compliance Checking for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
paper.abstract: When LLM agents exchange messages in a pipeline, abstractive compression discards task constraints. Routing tags get absorbed into prose, privacy fields get paraphrased, hard instructions get softened. Even exhaustive reminder-based prompting retains only 53% of required routing markers, as measured by RTD: constraint tokens are low-salience relative to task content and are dropped at generation step boundaries even when restated in full. We propose C2-FAIC (Contract-Claim Failure-Aware Inter-agent Compliance), which guards the handoff moment directly: it maintains task requirements in a contract ledger outside agent context and checks each candidate message before it enters the shared trace. On 916 task-metric slices across AgentCollabBench, C2-FAIC is strongest on tracer retention and cross-context leakage control, while also reducing instruction decay and claim propagation relative to no intervention. Critic agents remain stronger on pure IDR and CPR process scores, showing that contract enforcement and generic critique address different failure structures. Multi-agent reliability requires controlling what crosses communication boundaries, not only evaluating what the pipeline ultimately produces.

paper.title: SFT or RL for Tool-Calling Agents? A Controlled Study Across Data, Method, and Scale
paper.abstract: Limited controlled evidence exists on how training data, adaptation method, and model scale jointly affect tool-calling performance in language-model agents. We evaluate supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with LoRA, reinforcement learning (RL) via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and SFT followed by GRPO across six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, covering both in-distribution performance and cross-dataset transfer. SFT with LoRA is the strongest in-distribution method throughout the 0.6B–32B range and best in 15 out of 18 experimental settings. On cross-dataset transfer, the methods are closer: GRPO wins 29 out of 54 settings where training and test datasets differ, but its margin over SFT averages under one point, and SFT→GRPO is rarely strongest at either comparison. Dataset mixing gives consistently strong transfer while staying close to specialized in-distribution training, regardless of method. Additional analysis further confirms that LoRA outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning, demonstrating that LoRA better preserves pretrained agentic behavior.

paper.title: D-Mem: A Dual-Process Memory System for LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Driven by the development of persistent, self-adapting autonomous agents, equipping these systems with high-fidelity memory access for long-horizon reasoning has emerged as a critical requirement. However, prevalent retrieval-based memory frameworks often follow an incremental processing paradigm that continuously extracts and updates conversational memories into vector databases, relying on semantic retrieval when queried. While this approach is fast, it inherently relies on lossy abstraction, frequently missing contextually critical information and struggling to resolve queries that rely on fine-grained contextual understanding. To address this, we introduce D-Mem, a dual-process memory system. It retains lightweight vector retrieval for routine queries while establishing an exhaustive Full Deliberation module as a high-fidelity fallback. To achieve cognitive economy without sacrificing accuracy, D-Mem employs a Multi-dimensional Quality Gating policy to dynamically bridge these two processes. Experiments on the LoCoMo and RealTalk benchmarks using GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3-235B-Instruct demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. Notably, our Multi-dimensional Quality Gating policy achieves an F1 score of 53.5 on LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini. This outperforms our static retrieval baseline, Mem0 (51.2), and recovers 96.7% of the Full Deliberation’s performance (55.3), while incurring significantly lower computational costs. [Code will be released upon acceptance of the paper.]

paper.title: VISTA: A Versatile Interactive User Simulation Toolkit for Agent Evaluation
paper.abstract: Evaluation remains a critical bottleneck for interactive agent development. Existing evaluation methods often rely on static benchmarks, which fail to capture the dynamic, multi-step nature of agentic behavior and struggle to expose meaningful failure modes. While user-simulation-based evaluation offers a promising alternative, existing simulation frameworks suffer from two major limitations. First, they provide limited mechanisms for evaluating the quality and comprehensiveness of simulated interactions, making it difficult to assess whether a simulator sufficiently explores an agent’s capabilities and failure modes. Second, most frameworks are restricted to either UI-only actions or API-only actions, limiting their ability to model the full range of realistic user behaviors. To address these limitations, we propose VISTA, a Versatile Interactive user Simulation Toolkit for Agent evaluation.

paper.title: CoDA-NAS: Pattern Knowledge-Based Cross-Task Neural Architecture Search with LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Recent studies increasingly employ large language models (LLMs) for neural architecture search (NAS); however, they typically rely on in-context learning, struggle to turn past evaluations into accumulated knowledge, and often suffer from structural hallucinations. Motivated by the observation that a search process should systematically accumulate past experience to guide future exploration, we propose CoDA-NAS, a cooperative dual-agent framework that investigates natural language as a medium for structural knowledge. At the core of our framework is a pattern knowledge base (PKB) that extracts, validates, and maintains design patterns from evaluated architectures. These patterns are retrieved as soft priors to guide the searcher agent instead of memoryless generation. The searcher agent employs a structured reasoning constraint to tightly align the generated topological outputs with these semantic concepts, thereby mitigating hallucinations. To ensure empirical reliability, an integrated lightweight predictor agent provides independent numerical validation. By applying a t-test, statistically verified knowledge enters the PKB, effectively curbing the spread of incorrect rules. Experimental results show that under strict search limits, CoDA-NAS achieves competitive performance using only a local open-weights model. Furthermore, the extracted text-based patterns generalize well to new tasks, establishing natural language as a reliable and robust medium for transferring architectural knowledge.

paper.title: Disentangling Topology and Diversity in Multi-Agent LLMs for Multilingual Low-Resource Emotion Detection
paper.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems combine multiple inference calls, but prior work often confounds how calls are connected with how they are diversified. We study these factors independently: inference topology and source of inter-agent diversity. In a controlled 2 x 3 matrix, we cross parallel aggregation and sequential refinement with stochastic sampling, role prompting, and learned QLoRA specialization, under a fixed three-call budget and output protocol within each backbone. Using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we evaluate all six configurations on multilingual low-resource emotion detection across nine languages. Parallel learned specialization is strongest on Qwen at 52.83 Macro-F1 and reaches 52.94 on Llama. On Qwen it also exceeds same-backbone zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, and seven-call self-consistency baselines. The preferred topology depends on diversity source: sequential refinement helps stochastic and prompted settings, while the learned Width advantage shrinks from 2.83 points on Qwen to 0.17 on Llama. Depth-wise analysis suggests that later learned specialists can overwrite correct early predictions, although the aggregate effect is backbone-dependent. Overall, how agents are differentiated produces larger performance shifts than topology, which should be evaluated jointly with specialization.

paper.title: Teaching Coding Assistants What to Change: Fine-Tuning from Pairwise Preferences
paper.abstract: Real code-editing requests typically mix the target program with other related materials, such as test results or documentation. However, models often make mistakes by incorrectly changing these supporting materials or missing the actual code that needs correction. To investigate this issue, we created multiple task scenarios where the code needing changes and the intended behavior remained constant, while only the surrounding supporting texts varied. This approach allowed us to test if supporting texts that resemble code can confuse the model, making it difficult to identify the correct code to modify. To address this, we developed a simple yet effective training method by showing the model examples of correct and incorrect edits. Specifically, Correct examples only modify the intended code, whereas incorrect examples mistakenly alter or duplicate supporting texts. Our results suggest that reliable code editing depends on the model’s early ability to distinguish between guidance materials and the actual code requiring changes.

paper.title: Does The Way You Plan Matter? An Empirical Study of Planning Representations for LLM Web Agents

author.affiliation: McGill University and Mila - Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute

paper.abstract: Despite recent advances, LLM-based web agents still struggle with limited exploration, omission of critical steps, and sensitivity to task constraints. Prior work suggests that many of these failures stem from weaknesses in planning, yet the impact of alternative natural language plan representation remains unexplored. To address this, we introduce , a static planner-executor framework that evaluates the impact of plan representation in agent performance. We first automatically categorize WebArena tasks into 3 difficulty levels, enabling consistent difficulty grading without human annotation. Then we systematically evaluate 4 different plan representations on the tasks categorized as hard: sequential subgoals, narrative, pseudocode, and checklist; across different families of multimodal LLM powered agents (OpenAI, Alibaba, and Google). To account for stochastic variability, we introduce a novel decomposition of agent Success Rate (SR) into 2 interpretable evaluation metrics: Achievement Rate (AR) and Solved-Task Consistency (STC). Our results show that both, the plan formulation and the underlying LLM generating the plan, significantly influence web-agent robustness and task success. Code and dataset are available [here](https://github.com/alzambranolu13/plan-ahead).

paper.title: Prompting Strategies for Conceptual Ideation in Problem Solving

author.affiliation: Florida Institute for Human and Machine Cognition
The Institute for Human & Machine Cognition

paper.abstract: LLMs have improved at executing well-specified chains of reasoning but remain weak at conceptual ideation, which identifies what is worth reasoning about in the first place. We cast this as bilevel optimization over (i) a compact hypothesis space \Theta\subseteq\Theta_0 and (ii) a point \theta\in\Theta, and derive a domain-agnostic prompting strategy — Generate-\Theta — that makes hypothesis-space construction an explicit pre-solving step. On two challenging puzzle domains, Generate-\Theta matches or exceeds the max-thinking variant of the same base model (Claude Opus 4.6 or DeepSeek-v3.2/v4) and outperforms reasonable prompting baselines. These results suggest our method works well in tasks that are well-represented in the training set but nonetheless require creativity to solve new instances. Based on our formalism, we propose extensions for solving less familiar tasks as well. Results may provide insight into strategies learned by “reasoning” models during training. Our prompting strategy (or extensions thereof) could be integrated with RL training to produce better exploratory data for reasoning models in ideation-heavy tasks.

paper.title: Policy Loopholes in Agent Evaluation: When Policy Ambiguity Masquerades as Agent Error
paper.abstract: Agent benchmarks evaluate policy compliance but assume each policy determines a unique correct action. Natural-language policies can violate this assumption through silence, ambiguity, or contradiction, admitting multiple defensible readings that a single gold trajectory cannot capture. Auditing two \tau^2-bench domains, we develop a taxonomy of such policy loopholes and show that affected tasks produce unreliable scores: they lower scores across different models in different ways and make every model less consistent across repeated trials. A cross-domain comparison reveals that exploitability requires both policy ambiguity and tool permissiveness: when policy complexity exceeds what tools can enforce, agents resolve gaps inconsistently and scores become unreliable. Policy specification quality sets the ceiling on evaluation quality. Benchmark developers should audit policies before collecting gold annotations.

paper.title: ToolFuse: Documentation-Intent Fusion for Training-Free Tool Retrieval
paper.abstract: Tool retrieval is a necessary first step for tool-augmented LLMs once the set of available tools grows to thousands or more, and itscentral difficulty stems from two gaps. A user query states what the user wants to accomplish in task-centric language, whereas tooldocumentation describes functionality, parameters, and calling conditions in function-centric terms. This low lexical overlap produces aQuery-Documentation Mismatch. Complex queries also bundle several functional needs at once, while a single tool usually covers only one,producing a Multi-Intent Query Mismatch. We present ToolFuse, a training-free framework that addresses each gap on a different side ofretrieval. On the tool side, Complementarity-based Semantic Fusion treats tool documentation and LLM-generated synthetic intent as adocumentation view and an intent view of the same tool, encodes them separately, and assigns each tool a fusion weight from the geometriccomplementarity between its two views in vector space, without fine-tuning the frozen dense encoder. On the query side, QueryDecomposition splits a multi-intent query into focused sub-queries, retrieves for each, and aggregates the results with rank-aware round-robin. On ToolBench, the full ToolFuse raises the Per-Split average NDCG@5 of Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B from 64.72 to 75.49, with consistentgains across three additional dense encoder backbones.

paper.title: Trace2Ground: Scenario, Disambiguation, and Relation Traces for Web GUI Grounding
paper.abstract: We present Trace2Ground, a large-scale web GUI grounding dataset and benchmark built by parsing HTML/DOM to obtain candidate interface elements and using large language models to simulate interaction traces and natural-language instructions. Existing datasets primarily target instructions solvable by matching the target element’s visible text, while real-world GUI tasks may require grounding under user scenarios, duplicate candidates, and relational descriptions. Trace2Ground targets these under-explored stress regimes through three curated splits: PragmaMind, where instructions describe user scenarios without naming UI elements; ContextTwin, where multiple elements share identical visible text and the correct target must be selected using interaction context; and RelateLoc, where the target is specified via spatial or structural relations to nearby anchors. We construct the dataset via an automated pipeline that extracts candidates from HTML/DOM structure, synthesizes traces and instructions with LLMs, and applies multi-view visual checks. Strong specialist GUI grounders underperform on these regimes despite reaching around 90% on ScreenSpot, exposing a gap not addressed by existing GUI training data. Standard supervised fine-tuning on Trace2Ground improves the base model’s performance on our curated regimes by 42.3% on average and yields zero-shot transfer to standard GUI benchmarks, including a 9.8% average improvement on the non-web ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark across six desktop domains.

paper.title: Securing the Floor and Raising the Ceiling: A Merging-based Paradigm for Multi-modal Search Agents
paper.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have motivated the development of multi-modal search agents that can actively invoke external search tools and integrate retrieved evidence through multi-step reasoning. While promising, existing approaches typically rely on large-scale supervised trajectories or expensive reinforcement learning (RL), leading to high training cost, instability, and a severe cold-start problem for standard VLMs. We propose a training-free paradigm to empower VLMs with autonomous search capabilities via cross-modal model merging. By fusing a text-based search agent with a base VLM, we show that multi-modal search capabilities can be effectively composed without any additional multi-modal training data. To mitigate parameter interference during cross-modal integration, we introduce Optimal Brain Merging (OBM), a saliency-aware merging algorithm that identifies task-critical parameters based on their impact on model loss using only a small set of calibration samples. Extensive experiments on search-intensive benchmarks (e.g., InfoSeek, MMSearch) reveal that: (1) Model merging secures a reasonable performance floor as a zero-shot agent, with OBM achieving superior search rates; (2) OBM significantly raises the performance ceiling as a warm-start strategy, achieving faster convergence and higher peak accuracy than standard VLM initialization.

paper.title: CoHyDE: Iterative Co-Training of LLM Rewriter & Dense Encoder for Tool Retrieval
paper.abstract: Tool retrieval over large API catalogs is a core bottleneck for LLM agents: user queries arrive in colloquial, often underspecified language, while the catalog uses technical API vocabulary that no fixed encoder can bridge on its own. The two dominant training approaches, contrastive encoder fine-tuning and HyDE-style query expansion with a frozen LLM, address this problem from opposite ends and fail in complementary directions: the fine-tuned encoder excels when the query’s surface form already matches the catalog but collapses when it does not, while zero-shot HyDE is more robust to underspecified queries yet generates catalog-unaware hypothetical descriptions that degrade retrieval when queries are well-formed. We introduce CoHyDE, an iterative procedure that trains the dense encoder and the LLM rewriter as a single co-evolving system: the encoder is retrained with InfoNCE on catalog-style hypothetical descriptions produced by the rewriter, and the rewriter is preference-aligned via DPO against the encoder’s retrieval scores, with both sides warm-started on the tool catalog before the loop begins. On a 10k tool subset of the ToolBench catalog, three rounds of CoHyDE improve over the strongest single-component baseline by +2.5 pp NDCG@5 on standard queries and +6.3 pp on held-out vague queries, with gains as large as +8 pp on the hardest vague tier. Ablations confirm that co-training is the key ingredient: using either component in isolation fails to match CoHyDE on both well-formed and vague queries, with losses of up to -8 pp on vague queries.

paper.title: MATEO: A Multimodal Benchmark for Planning with Temporal Execution Ordering
paper.abstract: To achieve complex real-world goals, AI agents must be able to plan appropriate sequences of actions from a task specification. However, evaluating and improving the planning capabilities is challenging because planning involves multiple steps that are difficult to disentangle when viewed as a whole. A more feasible approach is to focus on Temporal Execution Order (TEO), a core planning sub-task that requires partially ordering actions based on dependency by reasoning about temporal and causal dependency constraints. Existing research studying models’ reasoning over temporal execution is limited to automatically derived annotations, approximations of TEO as a linear chain, or text-only inputs. To address this gap, we introduce MATEO (MultimodAl Temporal Execution Order), a multimodal benchmark designed to assess and improve the temporal reasoning abilities of Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs). We acquire a high-quality multimodal recipe corpus, authored through a standardized editorial process that decomposes instructions into discrete steps, each paired with corresponding images. We design a novel set of guidelines and procedures to collect TEO annotations as graphs via crowdsourcing, which can be extended to new recipes, languages, and domains. Using MATEO, we evaluate six state-of-the-art LVLMs across model scales, varying language context, multimodal input structure, and fine-tuning strategies, showing the importance of multimodal inputs as well as limitations of these models.

paper.title: Rethinking Agentic Search with RELEX: Is Lexical Retrieval Sufficient?
paper.abstract: Does a lexical retriever suffice as large language models (LLMs) become more capable within an agentic search loop? We revisit this question by pairing BM25 with increasingly capable LLMs and introduce Piika, a search agent equipped with three tools for retrieving, browsing, and reading documents. On the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, under the same GPT-5 + BM25 setup, Piika improves the accuracy from 58.3% to 74.6% while reducing cost from $400 to $95. Despite relying only on lexical retrieval, it also outperforms the previously reported GPT-5 + dense-retriever setup, which achieves 73.0% accuracy at $361. Piika further scales with stronger LLMs, reaching 83.1% answer accuracy and 94.7% surfaced-evidence recall with GPT-5.5. Across model families, our results show that simple lexical retrieval, coupled with capable LLMs, a lightweight harness, and an effective tool interface, can remain highly competitive with more complex retrieval systems. Source code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://piika.ai.

paper.title: CamPilot: A Multi-Agent Cinematic Assistant for Camera-Controlled Movie Generation
paper.abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into video generation has enabled rapid text-to-video creation and improved visual quality. However, it still falls short of professional filmmaking, where cinematographic language is less refined than human-crafted camera work and multi-shot continuity remains challenging. To address these limitations, we introduce CamPilot, a multi-agent framework that integrates cinematographic planning and camera-work control to produce more coherent, logically structured, and human-aesthetic movies. CamPilot adopts a GRPO-based learning paradigm to learn camera work planning from 14K real-world professional movies, internalizing motion patterns and composition principles that support reasoning over shooting techniques (e.g., camera angle, motion, and focal behavior) and cross-shot relationships for controllable camera-viewpoint generation. Multiple agents further collaborate and evolve to improve overall output quality. To support this work and further studies in this domain, we establish CamEval, a benchmark for evaluating camera work quality and cinematic engagement. Empirical results show that CamPilot outperforms state-of-the-art text-to-movie generation methods on cinematographic control and quality, highlighting the impact of professional camera design on movie generation.

paper.title: Whose Repair? A Multi-Loop Diagnostic of Interactive Alignment in Human–LLM Conversation
paper.abstract: Two conversations can end with equally correct answers while requiring unequal user effort. One system may correct its own prior error. Another may succeed only after the user restores an instruction, referent, or evidential standard. Output-focused evaluation can assign these trajectories the same result and overlook who performed the work required for recovery. We propose a framework for measuring this difference through observable repair sequences in conversations between humans and large language models. Extending Pickering and Garrod’s Interactive Alignment Model, the framework combines four concurrent functional loops (Grounding, Continuity, Negotiation, and Epistemic) with a structural classification of who initiates and resolves repair and a temporal hypothesis about expectation stabilization. It generates testable predictions about system self-repair, epistemic signaling, and phase-dependent repair cost. In a pilot analysis of 30 dialogues, two human annotators achieved substantial agreement under an earlier turn-level rubric (Cohen’s κ = .75). The analysis revealed category-boundary problems that motivate the revised sequence-level framework presented here. Its evidential scope is limited to annotation feasibility. The resulting account makes repair burden measurable and specifies the evidence required for future validation.
